chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: [Enter Chorus.]

CHORUS. In beautiful Verona, where our story takes place, two families of equal standing have reignited an ancient feud, and the violence between them stains the hands of ordinary citizens. From these two enemy households, a pair of star-crossed lovers are born, whose terrible misfortunes and deaths finally put an end to their parents' hatred. The doomed course of their love, marked by death from the start, and the relentless fury of their parents' conflict, which nothing but their children's deaths could end, is what we will show you in the next two hours on this stage. If you listen patiently, whatever we leave out, we will try our best to make up for.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 1 — A Public Place in Verona
paragraphs: [Enter Sampson and Gregory armed with swords and bucklers.]
SAMPSON. Gregory, I swear, we won't put up with any insults.
GREGORY. No, because then we'd be no better than coal carriers.
SAMPSON. I mean, if we get angry, we'll draw our swords.
GREGORY. Sure, while you're alive, try drawing your neck out of a noose.
SAMPSON. I'm quick to fight when I'm provoked.
GREGORY. But you're not quickly provoked to fight.
SAMPSON. Any dog from the house of Montague provokes me.
GREGORY. To be provoked is to move, and to be brave is to stand your ground. So if you're provoked, you run away.
SAMPSON. A dog from that house will provoke me to stand my ground. I'll take the upper hand over any man or woman from the Montagues.
GREGORY. That just shows you're a weak servant, because the weakest always get pushed aside.
SAMPSON. True, and that's why women, being the weaker sex, always get pushed to the wall. So I'll push Montague's men away from the wall and push his women up against it.
GREGORY. The quarrel is between our masters and us, their servants.
SAMPSON. It's all the same. I'll show myself a tyrant: after I've fought with the men, I'll be rough with the women. I'll cut off their heads.
GREGORY. The heads of the women?
SAMPSON. Yes, the heads of the women, or their virginity. Take it however you like.
GREGORY. The ones who feel it will have to take it the way it comes.
SAMPSON. They'll feel me as long as I can stand upright. And everyone knows I'm quite the man.
GREGORY. It's a good thing you're not a fish; if you were, you'd be a dried-out nobody. Draw your sword. Here come some of the Montagues.
[Enter Abram and Balthasar.]
SAMPSON. My weapon is out. Start a fight. I'll back you up.
GREGORY. How? By turning your back and running?
SAMPSON. Don't worry about me.
GREGORY. No, honestly, I'm worried about you!
SAMPSON. Let's make sure the law is on our side. Let them start it.
GREGORY. I'll frown at them as I walk by, and they can take it however they want.
SAMPSON. No, however they dare. I'll bite my thumb at them, which is an insult if they put up with it.
ABRAM. Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON. I am biting my thumb, sir.
ABRAM. Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON. Is the law on our side if I say yes?
GREGORY. No.
SAMPSON. No, sir, I'm not biting my thumb at you, sir. But I am biting my thumb, sir.
GREGORY. Are you looking for a fight, sir?
ABRAM. A fight, sir? No, sir.
SAMPSON. But if you are, sir, I'm ready for you. I serve a man as good as yours.
ABRAM. No better.
SAMPSON. Well, sir.
[Enter Benvolio.]
GREGORY. Say "better." Here comes one of my master's relatives.
SAMPSON. Yes, better, sir.
ABRAM. You're a liar.
SAMPSON. Draw your swords, if you're men. Gregory, remember your slashing blow.
[They fight.]
BENVOLIO. Stop, you fools! Put away your swords. You don't know what you're doing.
[Beats down their swords.]
[Enter Tybalt.]
TYBALT. What, you've drawn your sword among these cowards? Turn around, Benvolio, and face your death.
BENVOLIO. I'm only trying to keep the peace. Put away your sword, or use it to help me separate these men.
TYBALT. What, your sword is drawn and you talk of peace? I hate that word as much as I hate hell, all Montagues, and you. Have at you, coward!
[They fight.]
[Enter three or four Citizens with clubs.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Clubs, weapons, and spears! Strike! Beat them down! Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
[Enter Capulet in his gown, and Lady Capulet.]
CAPULET. What's all this noise? Give me my sword!
LADY CAPULET. A crutch, a crutch! Why are you calling for a sword?
CAPULET. My sword, I said! Old Montague is here, waving his blade to spite me.
[Enter Montague and his Lady Montague.]
MONTAGUE. You villain, Capulet! Don't hold me back. Let me go.
LADY MONTAGUE. You will not take a single step to find an enemy.
[Enter Prince Escalus, with Attendants.]

PRINCE. Rebellious subjects, enemies of peace, you who stain your weapons with your neighbors' blood! Will you not listen? Hey! You men, you beasts, you who put out the fire of your murderous rage with streams of blood pouring from your veins! On pain of torture, throw your weapons to the ground and hear the sentence of your angry Prince. Three times now, civil brawls started by a careless word, by you, old Capulet, and you, Montague, have disturbed the peace of our streets and forced Verona's elderly citizens to take up rusty old weapons in their aged hands to stop your rotten hatred. If you ever disturb our streets again, your lives will pay the price for breaking the peace. For now, everyone leave. You, Capulet, come with me. And Montague, come this afternoon to learn what further action I intend, to Old Free-town, our court of justice. Once more, on pain of death, everyone leave.
[Exeunt Prince and Attendants; Capulet, Lady Capulet, Tybalt,]
PRINCE. Citizens and Servants._]
MONTAGUE. Who started this old quarrel up again? Tell me, nephew, were you here when it began?

BENVOLIO. Your enemy's servants and yours were already fighting when I arrived. I drew my sword to separate them. At that moment, the hot-tempered Tybalt showed up with his sword ready, shouting insults at me. He swung his blade around his head and slashed at the air, which hissed at him in scorn. While we were trading blows, more and more people joined in on both sides, until the Prince came and broke it up.
LADY MONTAGUE. Oh, where is Romeo? Did you see him today? I'm so glad he wasn't in this fight.

BENVOLIO. Madam, an hour before dawn, when I was too troubled to sleep and went out walking, I saw your son under the grove of sycamore trees on the west side of the city. I headed toward him, but he spotted me and slipped away into the woods. I understood his mood because I felt the same way myself — wanting to be alone — so I didn't chase him and was glad to let him go.

MONTAGUE. Many mornings he's been seen there, adding his tears to the morning dew and his sighs to the clouds. But as soon as the sun begins to rise in the east and draw back the curtains of night, my gloomy son steals back home and shuts himself in his room, locks out the daylight, and makes himself an artificial night. This dark mood will lead to something bad unless someone can find the cause and help him.
BENVOLIO. My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
MONTAGUE. I don't know it, and I can't get him to tell me.
BENVOLIO. Have you tried everything to find out?

MONTAGUE. Both I and many friends have tried. But he keeps his own counsel and is so secretive, so shut off from any chance of understanding, like a flower bud eaten by a worm before it can open its petals to the sun. If we could learn where his sorrow comes from, we would gladly help cure it.
[Enter Romeo.]
BENVOLIO. Look, here he comes. Please step aside. I'll find out what's troubling him, or he'll have to refuse me outright.
MONTAGUE. I hope you're lucky enough to hear the truth from him. Come, my dear, let's go.
[Exeunt Montague and Lady Montague.]
BENVOLIO. Good morning, cousin.
ROMEO. Is it still so early?
BENVOLIO. It just struck nine.
ROMEO. Oh my. Sad hours seem so long. Was that my father who just left in such a hurry?
BENVOLIO. It was. What sadness is making your hours so long, Romeo?
ROMEO. Not having the thing that would make them short.
BENVOLIO. In love?
ROMEO. Out.
BENVOLIO. Of love?
ROMEO. Out of favor with the one I love.
BENVOLIO. It's sad that love, which looks so gentle, turns out to be so cruel in practice.

ROMEO. It's sad that love, which is blind, can still find its way into your heart! Where should we eat? Oh, never mind! What fight happened here? No, don't tell me. I've heard all about it. There's a lot to do with hate here, but even more with love. Brawling love! Loving hate! Something created out of nothing! Heavy lightness! Serious foolishness! Shapeless chaos made of beautiful forms! Lead feathers, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health! A waking sleep that isn't what it seems! This is the love I feel, and I find no love in it. Are you laughing?
BENVOLIO. No, cousin, I'd rather cry.
ROMEO. Why, good heart?
BENVOLIO. Because of your good heart's suffering.

ROMEO. That's what love does to you. My own sorrows weigh heavy on my chest, and your sympathy just adds more weight to mine. Love is a smoke made from the fumes of sighs. When cleared away, it's a fire sparkling in lovers' eyes. When troubled, it's a sea fed by lovers' tears. What else is it? A kind of dignified madness, a bitter poison, and a sweet medicine. Goodbye, cousin.
[Going.]
BENVOLIO. Wait! I'll come with you. If you leave me like this, you're doing me wrong.
ROMEO. Nonsense! I've lost myself. I'm not really here. This isn't Romeo. He's somewhere else.
BENVOLIO. Tell me seriously, who is it you love?
ROMEO. What, should I groan and tell you?
BENVOLIO. Groan? No. But seriously, tell me who.
ROMEO. Telling a sick man to seriously make his will is a cruel thing to say to someone who's so ill. Seriously, cousin, I love a woman.
BENVOLIO. I guessed that much when I figured you were in love.
ROMEO. Good guess, and she's beautiful.
BENVOLIO. A beautiful target, dear cousin, is easiest to hit.

ROMEO. Well, there you miss the mark. She won't be hit by Cupid's arrow. She has the wisdom of the goddess Diana, and she's well protected by her vow of chastity against love's weak little bow. She won't listen to sweet talk of love or meet the gaze of pursuing eyes or accept gold that could seduce a saint. She's rich in beauty, but her only poverty is that when she dies, all that beauty dies with her.
BENVOLIO. Then she's sworn to live without love forever?

ROMEO. She has, and by refusing love, she creates a huge waste. Beauty starved by her strictness means beauty is cut off from all future generations. She's too fair, too wise — wisely too fair — to earn heaven by making me miserable. She's sworn off love, and by that vow, I live as though already dead.
BENVOLIO. Take my advice: forget about her.
ROMEO. Oh, teach me how to stop thinking.
BENVOLIO. By letting your eyes look around. Check out other beauties.

ROMEO. That would only make hers seem more exquisite by comparison. Those beautiful masks that touch fair ladies' faces, being black, remind us of the beauty they hide. A man who goes blind can't forget the precious gift of sight he lost. Show me a woman who is extremely beautiful, and what does her beauty do except remind me of someone who surpasses her? Goodbye. You can't teach me to forget.
BENVOLIO. I'll prove that theory wrong, or die trying.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 2 — A Street
paragraphs: [Enter Capulet, Paris and Servant.]
CAPULET. Montague is bound by the same rules as I am, with the same penalties. I don't think it's hard for men as old as we are to keep the peace.
PARIS. You're both men of honorable reputation, and it's a shame you've been at odds for so long. But now, my lord, what do you say to my proposal?

CAPULET. I can only repeat what I've already said. My daughter is still young and inexperienced in the world. She hasn't even turned fourteen yet. Let two more summers pass before we consider her ready to be a bride.
PARIS. Women younger than her have already become happy mothers.

CAPULET. And those married so young are often ruined too soon. The earth has swallowed all my children except her. She is my one remaining hope. But go ahead and court her, gentle Paris. Win her heart. My consent depends on hers. If she agrees, then she has my blessing. Tonight I'm holding a party, an old tradition, and I've invited many guests, including people I care about. You're one more welcome addition. Come to my house tonight and you'll see stars walking on earth that make the heavens seem dark. You'll feel the same delight that young men feel when April, beautifully dressed, steps on the heels of limping winter. Among the lovely young women at my party, you'll find your share of joy tonight. Look at them all, see them all, and favor the one who deserves it most. Among the many, my daughter may be counted in number, though perhaps not stand out. Come with me. You there, go around Verona and find the people whose names are written here [gives a paper], and tell them my house and hospitality await their pleasure.
[Exeunt Capulet and Paris.]

SERVANT. Find the people whose names are written here! They say the shoemaker should stick to his measuring rod and the tailor to his needle, the fisherman to his paintbrush and the painter to his nets. But I've been sent to find the people whose names are written here, and I can't even read what's written. I'd better find someone who can. Oh, perfect timing!
[Enter Benvolio and Romeo.]

BENVOLIO. Come on, man. One fire burns out another. One pain lessens when you feel a different ache. Get dizzy and you'll be helped by spinning the other way. One hopeless grief is cured by another's suffering. Find a new love interest, and the poison of the old one will fade away.
ROMEO. A bandage leaf is great for that.
BENVOLIO. For what, exactly?
ROMEO. For your scraped shin.
BENVOLIO. Why, Romeo, are you crazy?
ROMEO. Not crazy, but more trapped than a madman is. Locked up in prison, starved, whipped, and tormented and — good evening, good fellow.
SERVANT. Good evening to you. Please, sir, can you read?
ROMEO. Yes, I can read my own miserable fortune.
SERVANT. Maybe you learned that without a book. But can you read anything you see written down?
ROMEO. Yes, if I know the letters and the language.
SERVANT. Fair enough. Have a good evening!
ROMEO. Wait, fellow. I can read.
[He reads the letter.]

ROMEO. Signior Martino and his wife and daughters; Count Anselmo and his beautiful sisters; the widow of Utruvio; Signior Placentio and his lovely nieces; Mercutio and his brother Valentine; my uncle Capulet, his wife and daughters; my fair niece Rosaline and Livia; Signior Valentio and his cousin Tybalt; Lucio and the lively Helena. A fine group. [Gives back the paper] Where are they supposed to go?
SERVANT. Up.
ROMEO. Up where? To supper?
SERVANT. To our house.
ROMEO. Whose house?
SERVANT. My master's.
ROMEO. I really should have asked you that first.
SERVANT. Now I'll tell you without you having to ask. My master is the great and rich Capulet, and if you're not from the house of Montague, please come and enjoy a cup of wine. Have a good evening.
[Exit.]

BENVOLIO. At this same old party of Capulet's, the beautiful Rosaline you love so much will be dining, along with all the most admired beauties of Verona. Go there and look at her with unprejudiced eyes. Compare her face with others I'll point out, and I'll make you think your swan is actually a crow.

ROMEO. If the devotion of my eyes ever sees such falsehood, then let my tears turn to fire and let my eyes, so often drowned in weeping yet never dying, be burned as liars. Someone more beautiful than my love? The all-seeing sun has never seen her equal since the world began.

BENVOLIO. Come on, you only think she's so beautiful because you've never compared her to anyone else. She's only been weighed against herself. But put her on a scale against some other woman I'll show you shining at this party, and she'll barely measure up compared to the one who now seems best.
ROMEO. I'll go along, but not to see anyone better. Only to rejoice in the splendor of my own love.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 3 — A Room in Capulet's House
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Capulet and Nurse.]
LADY CAPULET. Nurse, where's my daughter? Call her to me.
NURSE. I swear, on my virtue when I was twelve years old, I told her to come. Come here, lamb! Come here, little bird! Lord have mercy! Where is this girl? Juliet!
[Enter Juliet.]
JULIET. What is it? Who's calling?
NURSE. Your mother.
JULIET. Madam, I'm here. What do you need?
LADY CAPULET. This is what I want to discuss. Nurse, give us a moment alone. Actually, Nurse, come back. You should hear this too. You know my daughter is getting to be a young woman.
NURSE. I can tell you her age down to the hour.
LADY CAPULET. She's not yet fourteen.
NURSE. I'd bet fourteen of my teeth — and to my sorrow, I only have four — that she's not fourteen yet. How long is it until Lammas Day?
LADY CAPULET. Two weeks and a few days.

NURSE. Whether it's an even or odd number, of all the days in the year, on Lammas Eve night she'll be fourteen. Susan and she — God rest all Christian souls! — were the same age. Well, Susan is with God now. She was too good for this world. But as I was saying, on Lammas Eve she'll be fourteen. That she will, indeed. I remember it well. It's been eleven years since the earthquake. She was weaned that very day — I'll never forget it. I had put a bitter herb on my breast, sitting in the sun by the dovecote wall. You and my lord were in Mantua then. Oh, I have a good memory! When the baby tasted the bitterness and got fussy and fought with the breast! The dovecote shook from the earthquake; there was no need to tell me to get moving. That was eleven years ago. She could stand on her own by then. In fact, she could have run and toddled all over the place. Just the day before, she'd bumped her forehead. And then my husband — God rest his soul! He was a cheerful man — he picked up the child and said, "So, did you fall on your face? You'll fall on your back when you're older and wiser, won't you, Julie?" And the sweet little thing stopped crying and said, "Yes." It's funny how a joke comes full circle. I swear, if I lived a thousand years, I'd never forget it. "Won't you, Julie?" he said. And the sweet little thing stopped crying and said, "Yes."
LADY CAPULET. Enough of this. Please be quiet.

NURSE. Yes, madam, but I can't help laughing, to think how the baby stopped crying and said "Yes." And yet she had such a bump on her forehead, as big as a young rooster's stone. A terrible knock, and she cried so hard. "So," said my husband, "did you fall on your face? You'll fall on your back when you're older. Won't you, Julie?" And she stopped and said, "Yes."
JULIET. And you stop too, please, Nurse. Enough.
NURSE. All right, I'm done. God bless you. You were the prettiest baby I ever nursed. If I could live to see you married, that would fulfill my wish.
LADY CAPULET. Well, marriage is exactly what I came to talk about. Tell me, Juliet, how do you feel about getting married?
JULIET. It's an honor I haven't dreamed about.
NURSE. An honor! If I weren't your only nurse, I'd say you'd sucked wisdom from your mother's breast.

LADY CAPULET. Well, think about marriage now. Women younger than you, here in Verona, ladies of good standing, are already mothers. By my count, I was your mother at about the same age you are now. So here's the point: the brave and noble Paris wants you for his wife.
NURSE. What a man, young lady! Lady, such a man as the whole world could wish for. He's perfect, like a figure made of wax.
LADY CAPULET. Verona's summer hasn't produced a finer flower.
NURSE. Indeed, he's a flower. Truly, a very flower.

LADY CAPULET. What do you say? Can you love this gentleman? You'll see him tonight at our party. Study the beauty of young Paris's face and find the pleasure written there. Look at every handsome feature and see how each one enhances the others. Whatever remains hidden in this beautiful face, you'll find written in his eyes. This precious book of love, this unbound lover, only needs a cover to complete him. A fish belongs in the sea, and it's a great thing when an attractive exterior matches the beauty within. That book, admired in many people's eyes, that holds such a golden story in golden clasps — so you'll share everything he possesses by having him, without losing anything of yourself.
NURSE. Lose nothing? No, you'll gain. Women grow bigger through men.
LADY CAPULET. In short, can you see yourself loving Paris?
JULIET. I'll look to see if looking leads to liking. But I won't let my eyes go any further than your permission allows.
[Enter a Servant.]

SERVANT. Madam, the guests have arrived, dinner is served, someone's calling for you, someone's asking for my young lady, the Nurse is being cursed at in the kitchen, and everything is in chaos. I have to go attend to things. Please follow right away.
LADY CAPULET. We're coming.
[Exit Servant.]
LADY CAPULET. Juliet, the Count is waiting.
NURSE. Go, girl. May happy nights lead to happy days.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 4 — A Street
paragraphs: [Enter Romeo, Mercutio, Benvolio, with five or six Maskers;]
Torch-bearers and others.
ROMEO. Should we announce ourselves with a speech? Or should we just go in without any introduction?

BENVOLIO. That kind of elaborate entrance is out of date. We won't have any blindfolded Cupid carrying a painted bow, scaring the ladies like a scarecrow. No memorized prologue, nervously delivered with a prompter. Let them judge us as they will. We'll dance one dance and be gone.
ROMEO. Give me a torch. I'm not in the mood for dancing. Since I'm heavy-hearted, I'll just carry the light.
MERCUTIO. No, gentle Romeo, you have to dance.
ROMEO. Not me, believe me. You have dancing shoes with nimble soles. I have a soul made of lead that stakes me to the ground. I can't move.
MERCUTIO. You're a lover. Borrow Cupid's wings and fly above ordinary limits.
ROMEO. I'm too deeply pierced by his arrow to fly on his light feathers. I'm so weighed down that I can't jump above this misery. I'm sinking under love's heavy burden.
MERCUTIO. And if you sink into it, you'd be a burden on love. That's too much pressure for such a tender thing.
ROMEO. Is love a tender thing? It's too rough, too wild, too violent. It stings like a thorn.

MERCUTIO. If love is rough with you, be rough with love. Fight back against love's sting, and you'll beat it down. Give me a mask to cover my face. A mask over a face that's already a mask. What do I care if some nosy person spots my flaws? These thick eyebrows will do my blushing for me.
BENVOLIO. Come on, let's knock and go in. As soon as we're inside, everyone start dancing.

ROMEO. A torch for me. Let people with light hearts dance and tickle the floor with their heels. I'll follow the old saying: I'll be a wallflower and just watch. The fun was never meant for me. I'm done.
MERCUTIO. Oh, come on, don't be such a mouse. If you're stuck in the mud, we'll pull you out. Or from that swamp of love where you're stuck up to your ears. Come on, we're wasting daylight.
ROMEO. No, we're not. It's nighttime.

MERCUTIO. I mean, sir, by hesitating we're wasting time, wasting our torches for nothing — like lighting candles during the day. Take my meaning in the right spirit. Our good judgment is five times better than any of us can express.
ROMEO. And we mean well by going to this party. But it's not wise to go.
MERCUTIO. Why? May I ask?
ROMEO. I had a dream last night.
MERCUTIO. And so did I.
ROMEO. Well, what was yours?
MERCUTIO. That dreamers often lie.
ROMEO. In bed, asleep, while they dream things that come true.

MERCUTIO. Oh, then I see Queen Mab has visited you. She's the fairy midwife, and she arrives in a shape no bigger than a gemstone on a mayor's finger, drawn by a team of tiny atoms across men's noses as they sleep. Her wagon's spokes are made from long spider legs, the canopy from grasshopper wings. Her harnesses are the finest spider silk, her collars made from moonbeams. Her whip is a cricket's bone, the lash a thin strand. Her driver is a tiny gray-coated gnat, not half as big as a small worm picked from a lazy girl's finger. Her carriage is an empty hazelnut shell, made by the carpenter squirrel or the old grub, fairy coachmakers since time began. And in this tiny state she gallops night after night through lovers' brains, making them dream of love. Over courtiers' knees, making them dream of bowing. Over lawyers' fingers, making them dream of fees. Over ladies' lips, making them dream of kisses — though angry Mab often plagues those lips with blisters because their breath smells of candy. Sometimes she rides over a courtier's nose, and he dreams of sniffing out a political favor. Sometimes she tickles a priest's nose with a pig's tail, and he dreams of getting a bigger parish. Sometimes she drives across a soldier's neck, and he dreams of cutting foreign throats, of battles and ambushes and Spanish swords, of drinking contests five fathoms deep. Then suddenly drums pound in his ear, and he wakes with a start, swears a prayer or two, and falls back asleep. This is the same Mab who tangles horses' manes in the night and bakes the matted knots in dirty hair, which bring bad luck when untangled. This is the spirit that, when girls lie on their backs, presses down on them and teaches them how to bear weight, making them women who carry well. This is she —
ROMEO. Enough, Mercutio, enough! You're talking about nothing.

MERCUTIO. True, I'm talking about dreams, which are the children of an idle brain, born from nothing but empty fantasy. They're as thin as air and more changeable than the wind, which right now woos the frozen north and then, getting angry, blows away toward the rainy south.
BENVOLIO. This wind you're talking about is blowing us off course. Supper is over, and we'll get there too late.

ROMEO. I'm afraid we'll get there too early. Something tells me that some consequence still hanging in the stars will begin its terrible course tonight at this party and end the term of my short life through some awful, untimely death. But let God, who steers my course, guide me. Onward, gentlemen!
BENVOLIO. Beat the drum. Let's go.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 5 — A Hall in Capulet's House
paragraphs: Musicians waiting. Enter Servants.
FIRST SERVANT. Where's Potpan? He's supposed to help clear the dishes. He can barely handle a single plate!
SECOND SERVANT. When all the good manners fall to just one or two people, and their hands aren't even clean, that's a sorry state of affairs.

FIRST SERVANT. Get rid of the stools, move the sideboard, and watch the silverware. Do me a favor and save me a piece of marzipan. And if you care about me at all, tell the doorman to let in Susan Grindstone and Nell. Antony! Potpan!
SECOND SERVANT. Yes, boy, ready.
FIRST SERVANT. People are looking for you and calling for you in the great hall.
SECOND SERVANT. We can't be in two places at once. Let's hurry, boys. Look lively for a while, and the last man standing gets everything.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Capulet, &c. with the Guests and Gentlewomen to the Maskers.]

CAPULET. Welcome, gentlemen! Ladies whose toes aren't bothered by corns will have a dance with you. Ha! My dear ladies, which of you will refuse to dance? Any woman who acts coy, I'll swear she has corns. Am I right? Welcome, gentlemen! I remember the days when I wore a mask and could whisper sweet nothings in a beautiful lady's ear. Those days are gone, long gone. You are welcome, gentlemen! Come, musicians, play! Make room, make room! Let the girls dance!
[Music plays, and they dance.]

CAPULET. More light, you there! And clear away the tables. And put out the fire — the room is getting too hot. Well, this unexpected entertainment is quite welcome. Come, sit down, sit down, good cousin Capulet. You and I are past our dancing days. How long has it been since you and I last wore masks? CAPULET'S COUSIN. By Our Lady, thirty years.

CAPULET. What, man, it hasn't been that long! It was at Lucentio's wedding. Come next Pentecost, that'll be about twenty-five years. And we wore masks then. CAPULET'S COUSIN. It's been longer than that. His son is older, sir. His son is thirty.
CAPULET. Are you sure? His son was still a minor just two years ago.
ROMEO. Who is that lady there, on the arm of that knight?
SERVANT. I don't know, sir.

ROMEO. Oh, she teaches the torches to burn bright! She hangs on the cheek of night like a jewel sparkling against dark skin. She's too beautiful for this world, too precious for earth! She stands out among the other women like a white dove in a flock of crows. When the dance is done, I'll watch where she goes, and by touching her hand, bless my own rough one. Did my heart ever love before? My eyes say no! I never saw true beauty until tonight.

TYBALT. By his voice, that should be a Montague. Get me my sword, boy. How dare this lowlife come here, hiding behind a costume, to mock and sneer at our celebration? By the honor of my family, I would not consider it a sin to strike him dead.
CAPULET. What's going on, kinsman? Why are you so upset?
TYBALT. Uncle, that's a Montague, our enemy. A villain who's come here out of spite to make fun of our party tonight.
CAPULET. Is it young Romeo?
TYBALT. It is. That villain Romeo.

CAPULET. Calm down, gentle cousin, and leave him alone. He carries himself like a fine gentleman, and to tell the truth, Verona speaks well of him as a virtuous and well-mannered young man. I wouldn't insult him in my own house for all the wealth in this city. So be patient. Pay him no attention. That is my wish. If you respect my wishes, put on a pleasant face and drop that scowl. An angry look is inappropriate at a celebration.
TYBALT. It's appropriate when such a villain is a guest. I won't tolerate him.

CAPULET. He will be tolerated. Listen here, boy! I say he will be, do you hear me? Am I the master of this house, or are you? You won't tolerate him! Good God, you'll start a riot among my guests! You want to be the big man!
TYBALT. But uncle, it's a disgrace.

CAPULET. Enough! You're an insolent boy. Is that so? This attitude could get you in real trouble, let me tell you. You want to defy me? Well, it's about time I put you in your place. Well done, everyone! — You're a brat. Now be quiet, or — More light, more light! — For shame! I'll make you quiet. Come now, enjoy yourselves, everyone.
TYBALT. Being forced to be patient while my blood boils makes my whole body tremble with rage. I'll leave for now, but this intrusion, which seems harmless now, will turn to bitter poison.
[Exit.]
[To Juliet.] If I profane with my unworthiest hand]
ROMEO. This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this: my lips, like two blushing pilgrims, are ready to smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
JULIET. Good pilgrim, you're too hard on your hand. It shows proper devotion, nothing more. Pilgrims' hands do touch the hands of saints, and palm touching palm is a pilgrim's kiss.
ROMEO. Don't saints have lips, and pilgrims too?
JULIET. Yes, pilgrim, lips that they must use for prayer.
ROMEO. Then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do. They pray. Grant their prayer, so faith doesn't turn to despair.
JULIET. Saints don't move, even when they grant prayers.
ROMEO. Then don't move while I receive the answer to my prayer. And so, from my lips, through yours, my sin is washed away.
[Kissing her.]
JULIET. Then my lips now have the sin that they took from yours.
ROMEO. Sin from my lips? What a sweetly argued trespass! Give me my sin back.
JULIET. You kiss by the book.
NURSE. Miss, your mother would like a word with you.
ROMEO. Who is her mother?

NURSE. Well now, young man, her mother is the lady of this house. A good lady, wise and virtuous. I nursed her daughter, the one you were just talking with. Let me tell you, whoever can win her hand will be a rich man.
ROMEO. She's a Capulet? Oh no! My life is now in my enemy's debt.
BENVOLIO. Let's go. It's best to leave now, while things are good.
ROMEO. Yes, I'm afraid so. And that only adds to my unease.

CAPULET. No, gentlemen, don't leave just yet. We have a small treat coming. Is it really that late? Well then, I thank you all. Thank you, good gentlemen. Good night. More torches here! Come, let's go to bed. My word, it's getting late. I'll go get some rest.
[Exeunt all but Juliet and Nurse.]
JULIET. Come here, Nurse. Who is that gentleman over there?
NURSE. The son and heir of old Tiberio.
JULIET. Who's that one, the one going out the door?
NURSE. I think that's young Petruchio.
JULIET. Who's that one following him, the one who wouldn't dance?
NURSE. I don't know.
JULIET. Go find out his name. If he's married, my grave will be my wedding bed.
NURSE. His name is Romeo, and he's a Montague. The only son of your greatest enemy.
JULIET. My only love, born from my only hate! Seen too soon before I knew who he was, and known too late! What a monstrous thing love has done to me, that I must love a hated enemy.
NURSE. What's this? What's this?
JULIET. Just a rhyme I learned just now from someone I danced with.
[One calls within, 'Juliet'.]
NURSE. Coming, coming! Let's go. The guests have all left.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 1 — Near Capulet's Garden
paragraphs: CHORUS. Now his old desire for Rosaline lies on its deathbed, and a young new love is eager to take its place. The beauty he used to sigh and long for, now matched against tender Juliet, isn't beautiful anymore. Now Romeo is loved and loves in return, both equally bewitched by each other's looks. But he must plead his love to someone who is supposed to be his enemy, and she must steal love's sweet rewards from dangerous hooks. Being considered an enemy, he can't approach her to make the kind of vows that lovers swear. And she, equally in love, has even fewer chances to meet her new beloved anywhere. But passion gives them the power and the opportunity to meet, softening extreme hardship with extreme sweetness.
[Exit.]
[Enter Romeo.]
ROMEO. How can I go forward when my heart is here? Turn back, heavy body, and find your center.
[He climbs the wall and leaps down within it.]
[Enter Benvolio and Mercutio.]
BENVOLIO. Romeo! Cousin Romeo! Romeo!
MERCUTIO. He's smart. I'll bet he's snuck off home to bed.
BENVOLIO. He ran this way and jumped over this orchard wall. Call him, Mercutio.

MERCUTIO. I'll do more than call. I'll summon him! Romeo! Moody! Madman! Passionate! Lover! Appear looking like a sigh! Just speak one rhyme and I'm satisfied. Just cry "Oh me!" Just say "love" and "dove." Say one pretty word to the goddess Venus, one nickname for her blind son and heir, young Cupid, who shot so well when King Cophetua fell in love with the beggar girl. He doesn't hear, he doesn't move, he doesn't stir. The game is up, and I'll have to summon him properly. I summon you by Rosaline's bright eyes, by her high forehead and her red lips, by her delicate foot, slender leg, and trembling thigh, and the regions that lie close beside. Appear before us in your true form!
BENVOLIO. If he hears you, you'll make him angry.

MERCUTIO. This can't anger him. What would anger him is if I conjured up a rival in his lady's bedroom, leaving him standing there until she dismissed him. That would be spiteful. My invocation is fair and honest. I'm only trying to make him come out, using his mistress's name.
BENVOLIO. Come on, he's hidden himself among these trees to keep company with the night. His love is blind, and darkness suits it best.

MERCUTIO. If love is blind, it can't hit the target. Now he'll sit under a fruit tree and wish his girlfriend were that kind of fruit that girls laugh about in private. Oh Romeo, if only she were, and you a nice ripe pear! Romeo, good night. I'll go to my little bed. This open field is too cold for me to sleep in. Shall we go?
BENVOLIO. Let's go. There's no point looking for someone who doesn't want to be found.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 2 — Capulet's Garden
paragraphs: [Enter Romeo.]
ROMEO. He can joke about scars because he's never been wounded.
[Juliet appears above at a window.]

ROMEO. But wait — what light is that, breaking through that window? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun! Rise, beautiful sun, and kill the jealous moon, who is already sick and pale with envy that you, her attendant, are far more beautiful than she is. Don't serve the moon, since she's so jealous. Her pale green uniform is only worn by fools. Throw it off! It is my lady. Oh, it is my love! Oh, if only she knew how much I love her! She speaks, but she says nothing. What does that matter? Her eyes are speaking. I'll answer them. No, wait — she's not talking to me. Two of the brightest stars in heaven, having some business elsewhere, have asked her eyes to twinkle in their place until they return. What if her eyes were up there and the stars were in her head? The brightness of her cheek would outshine those stars the way daylight outshines a lamp. Her eyes in heaven would shine so brightly through the sky that birds would start singing, thinking it was morning. Look how she rests her cheek on her hand. Oh, if only I were a glove on that hand, so I could touch that cheek!
JULIET. Oh my.

ROMEO. She speaks! Oh, speak again, bright angel! You are as glorious to this night, appearing above me, as a winged messenger from heaven is to the upturned, wondering eyes of mortals who fall back to gaze at him when he rides upon the clouds and sails across the sky.
JULIET. Oh Romeo, Romeo! Why do you have to be Romeo? Deny your father and reject your name. Or if you won't, just swear you love me, and I'll stop being a Capulet.
[Aside.]
ROMEO. Should I keep listening, or should I speak up now?

JULIET. It's only your name that's my enemy. You are yourself, regardless of being a Montague. What is "Montague"? It's not a hand, a foot, an arm, a face, or any other part of a person. Oh, be some other name! What's in a name? The thing we call a rose would smell just as sweet by any other name. So Romeo would still be perfect even if he weren't called Romeo. Romeo, get rid of your name, and in exchange for your name, which is no part of who you really are, take all of me.
ROMEO. I'll take you at your word. Just call me "love," and I'll be baptized with a new name. From now on, I will never be Romeo again.
JULIET. Who are you, hidden in the darkness, stumbling onto my private thoughts?
ROMEO. I don't know how to tell you who I am by name. My name, dear saint, is hateful to me because it's an enemy to you. If I had it written down, I would tear the word to pieces.
JULIET. My ears haven't yet heard a hundred words from your lips, but I recognize the sound. Aren't you Romeo, a Montague?
ROMEO. Neither one, beautiful girl, if either one displeases you.
JULIET. How did you get here, and why? The garden walls are high and hard to climb, and this place means death for you, considering who you are, if any of my relatives find you here.
ROMEO. I flew over these walls on the wings of love. Stone walls can't keep love out, and whatever love can do, love dares to try. So your relatives are no obstacle to me.
JULIET. If they see you, they'll kill you.
ROMEO. There is more danger in your eyes than in twenty of their swords. Just look at me sweetly, and I'm protected against their hatred.
JULIET. I wouldn't want them to find you here for anything in the world.
ROMEO. I have the darkness of night to hide me from their eyes. And if you don't love me, let them find me. I'd rather die by their hatred than live without your love.
JULIET. Who told you how to find this place?

ROMEO. Love told me where to look. Love gave me the idea, and I gave love my eyes. I'm no navigator, but even if you were as far away as a distant shore washed by the farthest sea, I would risk everything for such a prize.

JULIET. You know the darkness hides my face. Otherwise a maiden's blush would color my cheeks because of what you've heard me say tonight. I'd love to stick to proper behavior and deny what I've said, but forget about propriety. Do you love me? I know you'll say yes, and I'll take your word for it. But if you swear, you might be lying. They say the gods laugh at lovers' broken promises. Oh gentle Romeo, if you truly love me, say it honestly. Or if you think I've been won too easily, I'll play hard to get and say no, so you'll keep pursuing me. But otherwise, not for anything. To be honest, fair Montague, I'm too fond of you, and you might think my behavior is too forward. But trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more faithful than those who are better at playing coy. I should have been more reserved, I admit, but you overheard my true feelings before I knew you were there. So forgive me, and don't think this openness means my love is shallow, just because the dark night revealed it.
ROMEO. Lady, I swear by that blessed moon up there, the one that silvers the tops of these fruit trees —
JULIET. Oh, don't swear by the moon, that fickle moon that changes every month. I'm afraid your love might prove just as changeable.
ROMEO. What should I swear by?
JULIET. Don't swear at all. Or if you must, swear by yourself, because you are the god I worship, and I'll believe you.
ROMEO. If my heart's dear love —

JULIET. No, don't swear. Although you make me happy, I can't take joy in this promise tonight. It's too sudden, too rash, too impulsive. Like lightning, which flashes and is gone before you can say "it's lightning." Sweet love, good night. This bud of love, ripened by summer's warm breath, may become a beautiful flower when we next meet. Good night, good night! May you find as sweet a rest and peace in your heart as the peace I feel in mine.
ROMEO. Oh, will you really leave me so unsatisfied?
JULIET. What satisfaction could you have tonight?
ROMEO. The exchange of your faithful vow of love for mine.
JULIET. I gave you mine before you even asked for it. And yet I wish I could give it again.
ROMEO. Would you take it back? Why, love?

JULIET. Only to be generous and give it to you again. And yet I only wish for what I already have. My generosity is as boundless as the sea, my love as deep. The more I give to you, the more I have, because both are infinite. I hear a noise inside. Dear love, goodbye!
[Nurse calls within.]
JULIET. Coming, Nurse! Sweet Montague, be faithful. Wait just a moment. I'll come back.
[Exit.]
ROMEO. Oh blessed, blessed night! I'm afraid, being in darkness, that this is all just a dream, too sweet and flattering to be real.
[Enter Juliet above.]

JULIET. Three words, dear Romeo, and then truly good night. If your love is honorable and your intention is marriage, send me word tomorrow through a messenger I'll arrange, telling me where and when you want to have the ceremony. I'll lay all my fortunes at your feet and follow you, my lord, throughout the world.
[Within.] Madam.]
JULIET. I'm coming! But if you don't mean well, I beg you —
[Within.] Madam.]
JULIET. I'll be right there! — then stop your pursuit and leave me to my grief. I'll send someone tomorrow.
ROMEO. So help my soul —
JULIET. A thousand times good night!
[Exit.]
ROMEO. A thousand times worse, to be without your light. Love goes toward love the way schoolboys leave their books — eagerly. But love away from love moves toward school with heavy steps.
[Retiring slowly.]
[Re-enter Juliet, above.]

JULIET. Psst! Romeo, psst! Oh, I wish I had a falconer's voice to call this beautiful hawk back to me! Being a captive, I can barely speak above a whisper. Otherwise I would tear open the cave where Echo lives and make her voice even more hoarse than mine by repeating my Romeo's name over and over.
ROMEO. It is my soul that calls my name. How sweet lovers' voices sound at night, like the softest music to listening ears.
JULIET. Romeo!
ROMEO. My dear?
JULIET. What time tomorrow should I send my messenger to you?
ROMEO. By nine o'clock.
JULIET. I won't fail. It will feel like twenty years until then. I've forgotten why I called you back.
ROMEO. Let me stand here until you remember.
JULIET. I'll keep forgetting, just to keep you standing there, remembering how much I love your company.
ROMEO. And I'll keep standing here, just to keep you forgetting, forgetting any other home but this.

JULIET. It's almost morning. I want you to go, but no farther than a spoiled child's pet bird, which she lets hop a little distance from her hand, like a poor prisoner in tiny chains, then pulls it back with a silk thread, so lovingly jealous of its freedom.
ROMEO. I wish I were your bird.
JULIET. Sweet, so would I. But I'd kill you with too much affection. Good night, good night! Parting is such sweet sorrow that I could say good night until it becomes morning.
[Exit.]

ROMEO. May sleep rest on your eyes and peace fill your heart. I wish I were sleep and peace, to rest so sweetly. Now I'll go to my confessor's cell, to ask for his help and tell him about my wonderful fortune.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 3 — Friar Lawrence's Cell
paragraphs: [Enter Friar Lawrence with a basket.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. The gray-eyed morning smiles on the frowning night, streaking the eastern clouds with light. The darkness stumbles away like a drunkard, retreating from the path of day made by the sun's fiery wheels. Now, before the sun lifts its burning eye to cheer the day and dry the damp dew of night, I must fill this basket of ours with harmful weeds and precious medicinal flowers. The earth is both nature's mother and its tomb; what serves as its grave is also its womb. From the earth, children of many different kinds grow, nursed at nature's breast. Many have excellent healing properties, none is without some good quality, and yet each is different. Oh, there is great and powerful grace in plants, herbs, stones, and their true qualities. Nothing so vile grows on the earth that doesn't give some special good back to it. And nothing so good that, twisted from its proper use, doesn't rebel against its true nature and become harmful. Virtue itself becomes vice when misapplied, and vice can sometimes be made honorable through the right action.
[Enter Romeo.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Inside the tender skin of this small flower, both poison and medicine dwell. Smelled, it refreshes every part of the body. Tasted, it kills every sense along with the heart. Two such opposing forces are always at war in human beings, just as in herbs — grace and base desire. And where the worse side dominates, the cancer of death quickly devours the whole person.
ROMEO. Good morning, Father.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Bless you! What sweet early voice greets me? Young man, being up so early suggests a troubled mind. Worry stays awake in every old man's eyes, and where worry lives, sleep never comes. But where untroubled youth with an unstuffed brain rests, golden sleep rules. So your being up early tells me something is disturbing you. Or if that's not it, then I've guessed correctly: our Romeo hasn't been to bed tonight.
ROMEO. That last part is true. But the rest I had was sweeter than sleep.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. God forgive sin! Were you with Rosaline?
ROMEO. With Rosaline, my holy father? No! I've forgotten that name and the sorrow that came with it.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. That's my good boy. But where have you been, then?

ROMEO. I'll tell you before you ask again. I've been feasting at my enemy's house, where someone suddenly wounded me, and I wounded her in return. Both our cures lie within your help and holy skill. I bear no hatred, blessed man, because my request also benefits my enemy.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Be straightforward, my son, and speak plainly. A confusing confession gets a confusing answer.

ROMEO. Then know plainly that my heart's dear love is set on the beautiful daughter of rich Capulet. As my love is set on hers, so hers is set on mine. Everything is arranged except what you must join together through holy marriage. When, where, and how we met, we courted, and exchanged vows, I'll tell you as we go. But I beg you, agree to marry us today.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Holy Saint Francis! What a change this is! Rosaline, whom you loved so dearly, so quickly abandoned? Young men's love lives not truly in their hearts but in their eyes. Good Lord, what a flood of tears you shed over Rosaline! How much salt water wasted on a love you never truly tasted! The sun hasn't yet cleared your sighs from the sky. Your old groans still ring in my ears. Look, right there on your cheek sits the stain of a tear that hasn't been washed away yet. If you were ever truly yourself, and these sorrows were real, they were all for Rosaline. And now you've changed? Then let me say this: women may well give in to weakness when there's so little strength in men.
ROMEO. You used to scold me for loving Rosaline.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. For being infatuated, not for loving, my student.
ROMEO. And you told me to bury that love.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Not to bury one love only to dig up another.
ROMEO. Please don't scold me. The woman I love now returns my love equally, grace for grace. The other didn't.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Oh, she could see that your love was just reciting lines without understanding them. But come, young waverer, come with me. For one reason I'll help you: this marriage might turn your families' hatred into pure love.
ROMEO. Oh, let's go right now! I'm in a rush.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Wisely and slowly. Those who rush often stumble.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 4 — A Street
paragraphs: [Enter Benvolio and Mercutio.]
MERCUTIO. Where the devil is Romeo? Didn't he come home last night?
BENVOLIO. Not to his father's house. I spoke with his servant.
MERCUTIO. That same pale, hard-hearted woman, Rosaline, torments him so much that he'll surely go mad.
BENVOLIO. Tybalt, old Capulet's nephew, has sent a letter to Romeo's father's house.
MERCUTIO. A challenge to a duel, I'll bet my life.
BENVOLIO. Romeo will answer it.
MERCUTIO. Any man who can write can answer a letter.
BENVOLIO. No, he'll answer Tybalt himself, accepting the challenge, since he's been dared.

MERCUTIO. Poor Romeo. He's already dead — stabbed through the heart by a pale woman's dark eyes, run through the ear by a love song, the very center of his heart split by the blind boy Cupid's arrow. And this is the man who's supposed to face Tybalt?
BENVOLIO. Why, what's so special about Tybalt?

MERCUTIO. More than a Prince of Cats. Oh, he's the bold master of all fighting techniques. He fights the way a musician plays from sheet music — keeping perfect time, distance, and rhythm. He takes his precise pauses, one, two, and the third thrust goes right into your chest. He's the absolute butcher of precision, a duelist, a duelist! A gentleman of the finest fencing school, an expert in the first and second causes for dueling. Ah, the legendary lunge, the backhand thrust, the killing blow!
BENVOLIO. The what?

MERCUTIO. A plague on these affected, lisping posers! These new trend-setters with their fancy accents. By God, Tybalt's a very good swordsman, a very brave man, and quite the ladies' man. Isn't it pitiful, old friend, that we should be afflicted with these strange pests, these fashion-mongers, these "excuse me" types, who are so obsessed with new styles that they can't sit comfortably on an old bench? Oh, their precious bones!
[Enter Romeo.]
BENVOLIO. Here comes Romeo! Here comes Romeo!

MERCUTIO. Looking gutted, like a dried herring. Oh flesh, flesh, you've turned into a fish! Now he's caught up in the romantic poetry that Petrarch was famous for. Laura, compared to his lady, was just a kitchen maid — though she had a better poet to write about her. Dido was a frump. Cleopatra a gypsy. Helen and Hero, hussies and harlots. Thisbe had nice eyes, maybe, but nothing special. Signior Romeo, good day! There's a French greeting to match your French-style trousers. You gave us the slip last night.
ROMEO. Good morning to you both. What slip did I give you?
MERCUTIO. The dodge, sir, the dodge. Don't you get it?
ROMEO. Forgive me, Mercutio. My business was urgent, and in a situation like mine, a man can be excused for being rude.
MERCUTIO. That's as much as saying your situation forces a man to bow at the waist.
ROMEO. Meaning, to bow politely.
MERCUTIO. You hit that nail right on the head.
ROMEO. A very polite interpretation.
MERCUTIO. Well, I am the very model of politeness.
ROMEO. The pink of it, you might say — pink as a flower.
MERCUTIO. Right.
ROMEO. Then my shoe is well decorated with flowers.
MERCUTIO. Good one! Follow this joke now until you've worn out your shoe, so that when the sole is worn through, the joke can survive even after the wearing, being solely singular.
ROMEO. Oh, that's a thin-soled joke, singular in its weakness!
MERCUTIO. Come between us, Benvolio. My wit is fading.
ROMEO. Use your spurs, use your spurs! Or I'll claim victory.

MERCUTIO. Well, if your wit runs wild like a goose chase, I'm done. Because you have more of the wild goose in one of your wits than I have in all five of mine. Was I keeping up with you on the goose?
ROMEO. You were never with me on anything except when you were being a goose.
MERCUTIO. I'll bite your ear for that joke.
ROMEO. No, good goose, don't bite.
MERCUTIO. Your wit is a very tart apple — a sharp sauce indeed.
ROMEO. And isn't sharp sauce well served with a sweet goose?
MERCUTIO. Oh, here's a stretchy wit, like kid leather, that stretches from an inch to a whole yard.
ROMEO. I stretch it for that word "broad," which, added to the goose, proves you're a broad goose far and wide.

MERCUTIO. Now isn't this better than moaning about love? Now you're being social, now you're being Romeo. Now you're what you truly are, through both skill and nature. This drooling love of yours is like a big simpleton, running around with his tongue out trying to hide his toy in a hole.
BENVOLIO. Stop there, stop there.
MERCUTIO. You want me to cut my story short against the grain?
BENVOLIO. Otherwise you'd have made your story too long.
MERCUTIO. Oh, you're wrong. I would have made it short. I'd reached the full depth of my story and meant to pursue the matter no further.
[Enter Nurse and Peter.]
ROMEO. What a sight! A ship, a ship!
MERCUTIO. Two of them! A man and a woman!
NURSE. Peter!
PETER. Yes?
NURSE. My fan, Peter.
MERCUTIO. Give it to her, Peter, to hide her face. The fan is prettier than what's behind it.
NURSE. God give you good morning, gentlemen.
MERCUTIO. God give you good afternoon, fair lady.
NURSE. Is it afternoon already?
MERCUTIO. It's no less, I tell you. The hand on the clock is right at the stroke of noon.
NURSE. Get away with you! What kind of man are you?
ROMEO. A man, gentlewoman, that God made, only for himself to ruin.
NURSE. Well said, honestly! "For himself to ruin," he says! Gentlemen, can any of you tell me where I can find young Romeo?
ROMEO. I can tell you, but young Romeo will be older by the time you find him than when you started looking. I'm the youngest of that name, for lack of a worse one.
NURSE. You speak well.
MERCUTIO. Oh, is the worst one "well"? Very well taken, indeed! Wisely, wisely.
NURSE. If you are he, sir, I'd like a private word with you.
BENVOLIO. She'll be inviting him to dinner.
MERCUTIO. A matchmaker! A matchmaker! Hey!
ROMEO. What have you found?
MERCUTIO. Not a rabbit, sir — unless it's a stale old rabbit in a Lenten pie, something gray and worn out before it's even finished.
[Sings.]

MERCUTIO. An old gray rabbit, an old gray rabbit, is decent enough during Lent. But a rabbit that's gray is too old to pay for when it grays before it's spent. Romeo, are you coming to your father's house? We'll have dinner there.
ROMEO. I'll follow you.
MERCUTIO. Farewell, old lady. Farewell, lady, lady, lady!
[Exeunt Mercutio and Benvolio.]
NURSE. Please, sir, who was that rude fellow, so full of his vulgar jokes?
ROMEO. A gentleman, Nurse, who loves to hear himself talk, and will say more in a minute than he'll stand behind in a month.

NURSE. If he says anything against me, I'll put him in his place, even if he were tougher than he is, and twenty more like him. And if I can't do it myself, I'll find people who can. The scoundrel! I'm not one of his loose women. I'm not one of his gang! And you just stood there and let that man insult me however he pleased!
PETER. I didn't see anyone take advantage of you. If I had, my sword would have been out in a flash. I'm as quick to draw as any man, if the cause is right and the law is on my side.

NURSE. Now, before God, I'm so upset that every part of me is shaking. That scoundrel! Listen, sir, a word with you. As I told you, my young lady asked me to find you. What she told me to say, I'll keep to myself. But first let me tell you, if you were to lead her on dishonestly, as they say, that would be very low behavior, since the young lady is so young. And so, if you were to deal dishonestly with her, it would truly be a terrible thing to do to any young lady, and very weak behavior. ROMEO. Nurse, give my regards to your lady and mistress. I swear to you —
NURSE. Bless her heart, and I'll tell her exactly that. Lord, Lord, she'll be so happy!
ROMEO. What will you tell her, Nurse? You didn't let me finish.
NURSE. I'll tell her that you swear to her, which, as I understand it, is a gentlemanly offer.
ROMEO. Tell her to find some way to come to confession this afternoon. There, at Friar Lawrence's cell, she'll be confessed and married. Here's something for your trouble.
NURSE. No, truly, sir. Not a penny.
ROMEO. Go on, I insist you take it.
NURSE. This afternoon, sir? Well, she'll be there.

ROMEO. And wait, good Nurse, behind the abbey wall. Within the hour, my servant will meet you there and bring you a rope ladder. Under cover of night, that ladder will carry me up to the height of my joy. Goodbye. Be trustworthy, and I'll reward your efforts. Farewell. Give my regards to your mistress.
NURSE. God in heaven bless you! But listen, sir.
ROMEO. What is it, my dear Nurse?
NURSE. Can your servant keep a secret? Haven't you heard the saying: two can keep a secret if one of them is gone?
ROMEO. I guarantee my servant is as reliable as steel.

NURSE. Well, sir, my mistress is the sweetest lady. Lord, Lord! When she was a little chattering thing — Oh, there's a nobleman in town, a Count Paris, who'd love to get his hooks into her. But she, sweet soul, would rather see a toad, an actual toad, than see him. Sometimes I tease her and tell her Paris is the better man, but I assure you, when I say that, she turns as pale as a sheet. Don't rosemary and Romeo both start with the same letter?
ROMEO. Yes, Nurse. What of it? They both start with R.
NURSE. Ha! Joker! That's the dog's letter. R is for the — no, I know it starts with some other letter. And she has the prettiest little saying about you and rosemary that would do you good to hear.
ROMEO. Give my regards to your lady.
NURSE. Yes, a thousand times! Peter!
[Exit Romeo.]
PETER. Yes?
NURSE. Lead the way, and quickly!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 5 — Capulet's Garden
paragraphs: [Enter Juliet.]

JULIET. The clock struck nine when I sent the Nurse. She promised to be back in half an hour. Maybe she can't find him. That can't be it. Oh, she's so slow! Love's messengers should be thoughts, which fly ten times faster than sunbeams, chasing shadows across the hills. That's why swift-winged doves pull the chariot of love, and that's why Cupid has wings. The sun is at its highest point now, and from nine to twelve is three long hours, and she's still not back. If she had the energy and warm blood of youth, she'd move as fast as a ball. My words would bounce her to my sweet love, and his words back to me. But old people — so many of them move as if they were dead. Slow, heavy, and pale as lead.
[Enter Nurse and Peter.]
JULIET. Oh God, here she comes! Oh, sweet Nurse, what news? Have you met with him? Send your man away.
NURSE. Peter, wait at the gate.
[Exit Peter.]

JULIET. Now, good sweet Nurse — Oh Lord, why do you look so sad? Even if the news is bad, tell it cheerfully. If it's good, you're ruining the sweet music of good news by playing it with such a sour face.
NURSE. I'm exhausted. Give me a moment to catch my breath. Oh, how my bones ache! What a trip I've had!
JULIET. I wish you had my bones and I had your news. Come on, please, speak! Good, good Nurse, speak!
NURSE. Lord, such impatience! Can't you wait a moment? Can't you see I'm out of breath?

JULIET. How can you be out of breath when you have enough breath to tell me you're out of breath? The excuse you're making for delaying is taking longer than the actual news. Is it good or bad? Just answer that much. Say one or the other, and I'll wait for the details. Just tell me — is it good or bad?

NURSE. Well, you've made a simple choice. You don't know how to pick a man. Romeo? No, not him. Though his face is better than any man's, and his legs are the finest, and his hands and feet and body, though they're not worth bragging about, are beyond compare. He's not the most polished gentleman, but I guarantee he's gentle as a lamb. Go on your way, girl, and serve God. By the way, have you eaten?
JULIET. No, no! But I already knew all that. What does he say about our marriage? What about that?

NURSE. Lord, how my head aches! What a headache I have! It's pounding like it's going to split into twenty pieces. And my back — oh, my back, my back! Curse your heart for sending me running around town to catch my death.
JULIET. I'm truly sorry you're not feeling well. Sweet, sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me, what does my love say?
NURSE. Your love says, like an honest gentleman, and a courteous one, and a kind one, and a handsome one, and a virtuous one, I'm sure — Where is your mother?
JULIET. Where is my mother? She's inside, of course. Where else would she be? What a strange answer! "Your love says, like an honest gentleman, 'Where is your mother?'"
NURSE. Oh, for heaven's sake! Are you so impatient? Well then! Is this the thanks I get for my aching bones? From now on, deliver your own messages.
JULIET. What a fuss! Come on, what does Romeo say?
NURSE. Do you have permission to go to confession today?
JULIET. I do.

NURSE. Then hurry to Friar Lawrence's cell. There's a husband waiting to make you a wife. Now look at the color rushing to your cheeks — they'll be scarlet at any news. Hurry to the church. I have to go a different way, to get a ladder that your love will climb tonight to reach your window. I'm the drudge who does all the work for your happiness, but you'll carry the weight tonight. Go! I'll head to dinner. You go to the cell.
JULIET. Off to my great fortune! Thank you, dear Nurse. Farewell!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 6 — Friar Lawrence's Cell
paragraphs: [Enter Friar Lawrence and Romeo.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. May the heavens smile on this holy act so that no sorrow follows to scold us later.

ROMEO. Amen, amen! But let whatever sorrow come, it can't outweigh the joy that even one short minute in her presence gives me. Just join our hands with holy words, and then let death itself do what it dares. It's enough that I can call her mine.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. These passionate pleasures have passionate ends and die in their moment of triumph — like fire meeting gunpowder, which is consumed by the very kiss that ignites it. The sweetest honey becomes sickening in its own richness and destroys the appetite for more. So love moderately. Long-lasting love does. Arriving too fast ends up the same as arriving too slow.
[Enter Juliet.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Here comes the lady. Oh, what a light step! A foot so light will never wear out the eternal stone. A lover could walk on gossamer threads floating in the summer air and never fall — that's how weightless happiness is.
JULIET. Good evening, my holy confessor.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Romeo will thank you on behalf of us both, daughter.
JULIET. And the same to him, or else his thanks are more than I deserve.

ROMEO. Ah, Juliet, if the fullness of your joy is heaped as high as mine, and if you have more skill to express it, then sweeten the air around us with your voice and let the rich music of your words describe the happiness we both feel in this precious meeting.

JULIET. True feeling is richer in substance than in words. Those who brag about their feelings show off the surface, not the depth. Only beggars can count their worth. My true love has grown so great that I can't add up even half my wealth.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Come, come with me, and we'll be quick about this. Because, with your permission, you won't be left alone until the holy church makes two into one.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 1 — A Public Place
paragraphs: [Enter Mercutio, Benvolio, Page and Servants.]
BENVOLIO. Please, Mercutio, let's go home. It's a hot day, the Capulets are out and about, and if we run into them, there'll be a fight for sure. In this heat, everyone's blood is up.

MERCUTIO. You're like one of those fellows who walks into a bar, slaps his sword on the table, and says, "God grant I don't need this!" — and by his second drink, he's drawn it on the bartender, when there was no need for it at all.
BENVOLIO. Am I really like that?
MERCUTIO. Come on, you're as hot-tempered as any man in Italy. You're as quick to get angry and as quick to be set off.
BENVOLIO. And then what?

MERCUTIO. Well, if there were two of you, we'd soon have none, because you'd kill each other. You? You'd pick a fight with a man for having one hair more or less in his beard than you. You'd fight a man for cracking nuts, just because you have hazel-colored eyes. What kind of eyes would spot such a quarrel? Your head is as full of fights as an egg is full of meat, and yet your head has been beaten as scrambled as an egg from all the fighting. You've quarreled with a man for coughing in the street because he woke up your dog sleeping in the sun. Didn't you pick a fight with a tailor for wearing his new jacket before Easter? And with another for tying his new shoes with old laces? And you want to lecture me about quarreling!
BENVOLIO. If I were as quick to quarrel as you, any man could buy my life insurance for an hour and fifteen minutes.
MERCUTIO. An hour and fifteen minutes? Simple!
[Enter Tybalt and others.]
BENVOLIO. I swear, here come the Capulets.
MERCUTIO. By my heel, I don't care.
TYBALT. Stay close behind me, because I'm going to speak to them. Good afternoon, gentlemen. A word with one of you.
MERCUTIO. Just one word with one of us? Pair it with something else. Make it a word and a blow.
TYBALT. You'll find me ready enough for that, sir, if you give me a reason.
MERCUTIO. Can't you find a reason without being given one?
TYBALT. Mercutio, you hang around with Romeo.

MERCUTIO. "Hang around"? What, do you think we're musicians? If you make us out to be musicians, expect to hear nothing but discords. Here's my fiddle bow — here's what will make you dance. God's blood — "hang around"!
BENVOLIO. We're talking in a public place. Either go somewhere private to settle your grievances calmly, or just leave. Everyone's watching us.
MERCUTIO. Men's eyes were made to look, so let them watch. I will not budge for any man's convenience.
[Enter Romeo.]
TYBALT. Well, peace be with you, sir. Here comes the man I'm looking for.
MERCUTIO. I'll be damned if he's your servant, sir. Go ahead to the dueling field, and he'll follow. In that sense, you can call him your man.
TYBALT. Romeo, the love I have for you can offer no better greeting than this: you are a villain.
ROMEO. Tybalt, the reason I have to love you excuses the anger that such a greeting would normally provoke. I am no villain. So farewell. I can see you don't know who I really am.
TYBALT. Boy, this won't excuse the offenses you've committed against me. Turn and draw your sword.

ROMEO. I swear, I've never wronged you. In fact, I love you more than you can imagine, until you learn the reason for my love. And so, good Capulet — a name I treasure as much as my own — be satisfied.
MERCUTIO. Oh, what calm, dishonorable, vile submission!
[Draws.] Alla stoccata carries it away.]
MERCUTIO. Tybalt, you rat-catcher, will you come fight?
TYBALT. What do you want with me?

MERCUTIO. Good King of Cats, nothing but one of your nine lives. I intend to take that one, and depending on how you treat me afterward, I'll beat the other eight out of you. Will you draw your sword from its scabbard by the ears? Hurry, before mine is at your ears first.
[Drawing.] I am for you.]
ROMEO. Gentle Mercutio, put your sword away.
MERCUTIO. Come on, sir. Give me your best thrust!
[They fight.]

ROMEO. Draw, Benvolio! Knock their weapons down! Gentlemen, for shame, stop this outrage! Tybalt! Mercutio! The Prince has specifically forbidden fighting in Verona's streets! Stop, Tybalt! Stop, Mercutio!
[Exeunt Tybalt with his Partizans.]
MERCUTIO. I'm hurt. A plague on both your houses! I'm done for. Is he gone? Did he get away unscathed?
BENVOLIO. What, are you hurt?
MERCUTIO. Yes, yes. A scratch, a scratch. But it's enough. Where's my page? Go, boy, fetch a surgeon.
[Exit Page.]
ROMEO. Courage, man. The wound can't be that bad.

MERCUTIO. No, it's not as deep as a well or as wide as a church door, but it's enough. It'll do the job. Ask for me tomorrow and you'll find me a grave man. I'm finished, I'm sure of it. A plague on both your houses! God! A dog, a rat, a mouse, a cat — to scratch a man to death! A braggart, a scoundrel, a villain who fights by the textbook! Why the devil did you come between us? I was stabbed under your arm.
ROMEO. I thought I was doing the right thing.
MERCUTIO. Help me into some house, Benvolio, or I'll faint. A plague on both your houses! They've made worm food out of me. I'm done for, truly done. Your houses!
[Exeunt Mercutio and Benvolio.]

ROMEO. This gentleman, a close relative of the Prince and my very dear friend, has received a mortal wound on my behalf. My reputation is stained by Tybalt's insult — Tybalt, who has been my cousin for just one hour. Oh sweet Juliet, your beauty has made me soft and weakened the steel of my courage.
[Re-enter Benvolio.]
BENVOLIO. Oh Romeo, Romeo! Brave Mercutio is dead. That gallant spirit has risen to the clouds, scorning the earth too soon.
ROMEO. This day's dark fate will cast its shadow over days to come. This is only the beginning of sorrows that others must see through to the end.
[Re-enter Tybalt.]
BENVOLIO. Here comes the furious Tybalt, back again.

ROMEO. Back again, triumphant, and Mercutio killed? Away with gentle restraint! Let fire-eyed fury guide me now! Tybalt, take back the word "villain" that you gave me before. Mercutio's soul is hovering just above our heads, waiting for yours to keep him company. Either you, or I, or both of us must join him.
TYBALT. You miserable boy, you who kept company with him here — you'll go with him now.
ROMEO. This will decide that.
[They fight; Tybalt falls.]
BENVOLIO. Romeo, get away! Run! The citizens are coming, and Tybalt is dead. Don't stand there stunned! The Prince will sentence you to death if you're caught. Go! Be gone! Get away!
ROMEO. Oh, I am fortune's fool!
BENVOLIO. Why are you still standing here?
[Exit Romeo.]
[Enter Citizens.]
FIRST CITIZEN. Which way did the man who killed Mercutio go? Tybalt, that murderer — which way did he run?
BENVOLIO. Tybalt is lying right there.
FIRST CITIZEN. Get up, sir, come with me. I order you, in the Prince's name, to obey.
[Enter Prince, attended; Montague, Capulet, their Wives and others.]
PRINCE. Where are the vile people who started this fight?
BENVOLIO. Oh noble Prince, I can tell you everything about how this fatal brawl went wrong. That man lying there was killed by young Romeo. He's the same one who killed your kinsman, brave Mercutio.

LADY CAPULET. Tybalt, my cousin! Oh, my brother's child! Oh Prince! Oh husband! The blood of my dear relative has been spilled! Prince, as you are just, demand that Montague blood be shed for ours. Oh cousin, cousin!
PRINCE. Benvolio, who started this bloody fight?

BENVOLIO. Tybalt, who lies dead here, slain by Romeo's hand. Romeo spoke to him fairly and urged him to think about how trivial the quarrel was, reminding him of your displeasure. All of this was said in a gentle tone, with a calm expression and with humble bowing. But it couldn't make peace with Tybalt's uncontrollable anger. Deaf to any call for peace, Tybalt lunged with his sword at bold Mercutio's chest. Mercutio, equally fired up, matched him blow for blow. With one hand he knocked death aside, and with the other sent it back at Tybalt, whose skill returned it. Romeo cried aloud, "Stop, friends! Friends, stop!" And faster than his words, his quick arm knocked their deadly blades down. He rushed between them, and from under his arm, a spiteful thrust from Tybalt struck brave Mercutio's heart. Then Tybalt ran. But soon he came back to find Romeo, who had just tasted the desire for revenge. They went at each other like lightning. Before I could draw my sword to separate them, Tybalt was dead. And as he fell, Romeo turned and fled. This is the truth, or let me die.

LADY CAPULET. He's a relative of the Montagues. His loyalty makes him lie; he's not telling the truth. Some twenty of them fought in this bloody clash, and all twenty could only manage to kill one man. I demand justice, Prince, which you must deliver. Romeo killed Tybalt. Romeo must die.
PRINCE. Romeo killed Tybalt, and Tybalt killed Mercutio. Who now owes the price for Mercutio's precious blood?
MONTAGUE. Not Romeo, Prince. He was Mercutio's friend. His only fault was finishing what the law would have demanded anyway — the life of Tybalt.

PRINCE. And for that offense, I immediately banish him from Verona. I have a personal stake in your hatred's consequences — my own kinsman's blood was shed in your senseless brawls. But I'll punish you with such a heavy fine that you'll all regret what I've lost. I will be deaf to pleading and excuses. Neither tears nor prayers will buy forgiveness for these crimes. So don't bother. Let Romeo leave at once. If he's found here after this, that moment will be his last. Carry this body away and await my further orders. Showing mercy to murderers only creates more murder.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 2 — A Room in Capulet's House
paragraphs: [Enter Juliet.]

JULIET. Race faster, you fiery horses of the sun, toward the western horizon. A driver like Phaeton would whip you into the west and bring dark night immediately. Spread your curtain, loving night, so that no prying eyes can see, and Romeo can leap into my arms unnoticed and unseen. Lovers can see well enough to perform their acts of love by their own beauty. Or if love is blind, all the better — it suits the darkness. Come, sober night, dressed all in black, and teach me how to win by losing, playing for a pair of untouched maidenheads. Cover the wild blood rushing to my cheeks with your dark cloak, until shy love grows bold and sees that true love acted upon is simply innocent devotion. Come, night! Come, Romeo! You day within the night! You will lie upon the wings of night, whiter than fresh snow on a raven's back. Come, gentle night. Come, loving, dark-browed night. Give me my Romeo. And when I die, take him and cut him into little stars, and he will make the face of heaven so beautiful that the whole world will fall in love with the night and stop worshiping the garish sun. Oh, I have bought the mansion of love but haven't moved in yet. I've been sold but not yet enjoyed. The wait is as unbearable as the night before a holiday to an impatient child who has new clothes and isn't allowed to wear them yet. Oh, here comes my Nurse. She brings news! And every voice that speaks anything other than Romeo's name is as nothing compared to his heavenly eloquence.
[Enter Nurse, with cords.]
JULIET. Now, Nurse, what news? What do you have there? The rope ladder that Romeo asked you to get?
NURSE. Yes, yes, the ropes.
[Throws them down.]
JULIET. Oh no, what news? Why are you wringing your hands?
NURSE. Oh, what a terrible day! He's dead, he's dead, he's dead! We're ruined, my lady, we're ruined! Oh, the horror! He's gone, he's been killed, he's dead!
JULIET. Can heaven be so cruel?
NURSE. Romeo can be, even if heaven can't. Oh Romeo, Romeo! Who would have ever thought it? Romeo!

JULIET. What kind of devil are you, to torment me like this? This torture belongs in the depths of hell. Has Romeo killed himself? Just say yes, and that one small word will poison me more than the deadly gaze of a serpent. I am not myself if such a thing is true. Or else those eyes are shut that would make you answer yes. If he's dead, say yes. If not, say no. One short word will determine my happiness or my despair.
NURSE. I saw the wound with my own eyes — God help us! — right here on his manly chest. A pitiful corpse, a bloody pitiful corpse. Pale, pale as ashes, all smeared with blood. I fainted at the sight.

JULIET. Oh, break, my heart! Poor bankrupt heart, break at once! Eyes, go to prison and never look on freedom again. Return to dust, wretched body. Let all movement end, and let Romeo and me share one heavy funeral bed.
NURSE. Oh Tybalt, Tybalt! The best friend I ever had! Oh courteous Tybalt, honest gentleman! That I should live to see you dead!

JULIET. What storm is this, blowing in opposite directions? Is Romeo killed and Tybalt dead? My dearest cousin and my dearer husband? Then sound the trumpet of doom, because who is left alive if those two are gone?
NURSE. Tybalt is dead, and Romeo is banished. Romeo killed him, and Romeo has been banished.
JULIET. Oh God! Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?
NURSE. It did, it did! Oh, what a terrible day!

JULIET. Oh, a serpent's heart hidden behind a beautiful face! Did a dragon ever guard such a lovely cave? Beautiful tyrant! Angelic fiend! A dove-feathered raven! A wolf in lamb's clothing! A despicable thing dressed in divine beauty! The exact opposite of what you seemed to be — a damned saint, an honorable villain! Oh nature, what were you doing in hell when you placed the spirit of a demon inside such beautiful flesh? Was there ever a book containing such vile content so beautifully bound? Oh, that deception should live in such a gorgeous palace!

NURSE. You can't trust men. None of them. All liars, all oath-breakers, all worthless, all deceivers. Oh, where's my servant? Give me some brandy! These griefs, these sorrows make me old. Shame on Romeo!

JULIET. May your tongue blister for saying that! He was not born for shame. Shame itself is ashamed to sit on his brow, because it's a throne where honor should be crowned as the sole ruler of the entire earth. Oh, what a beast I was to criticize him!
NURSE. Will you speak well of the man who killed your cousin?

JULIET. Should I speak ill of the man who is my husband? Oh, my poor lord, what voice can speak well of your name when I, your wife of only three hours, have torn it apart? But why, villain, did you kill my cousin? That villain cousin would have killed my husband. Back, foolish tears, back to where you came from! Your drops belong to sorrow, but you're mistakenly offering them to joy. My husband is alive, whom Tybalt would have killed. And Tybalt is dead, who would have killed my husband. All of this should comfort me. So why am I crying? There was some word, worse than Tybalt's death, that destroyed me. I wish I could forget it, but oh, it presses on my memory the way guilty deeds haunt sinners' minds. "Tybalt is dead, and Romeo is banished." That word "banished" has killed ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt's death alone would have been grief enough.
