Or if grief loves company and must be paired with other sorrows, why didn't she follow Tybalt's death with news of my father's or mother's death, or even both? That would have been normal grief. But following Tybalt's death with "Romeo is banished" — to speak that word is like saying father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet, all killed, all dead. "Romeo is banished" — there is no end, no limit, no measure to the death contained in that word. No words can express that grief. Where are my father and mother, Nurse?
NURSE. Weeping and wailing over Tybalt's body. Do you want to go to them? I'll take you there.

JULIET. Let them wash his wounds with their tears. Mine will be saved for Romeo's banishment, when theirs have dried up. Pick up those ropes. Poor ropes, you've been cheated, and so have I. Romeo is exiled. He made you into a highway to my bed, but I, a maiden, will die a maiden-widow. Come, ropes. Come, Nurse. I'll go to my wedding bed, and let death, not Romeo, be my bridegroom.
NURSE. Go to your room. I'll find Romeo to comfort you. I know exactly where he is. Listen — your Romeo will come to you tonight. I'll go to him. He's hiding at Friar Lawrence's cell.
JULIET. Oh, find him! Give this ring to my true love and tell him to come for his last farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 3 — Friar Lawrence's Cell
paragraphs: [Enter Friar Lawrence.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Romeo, come out! Come out, you frightened man. Misery has fallen in love with you, and you are married to disaster.
[Enter Romeo.]
ROMEO. Father, what news? What is the Prince's sentence? What new sorrow is reaching for me that I don't yet know about?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. You're too well acquainted with that kind of bitter company, my dear son. I bring you news of the Prince's sentence.
ROMEO. What less than doomsday could the Prince's sentence be?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. A gentler judgment came from his lips. Not death, but banishment.
ROMEO. Ha! Banishment? Be merciful and say death instead! Exile holds more terror than death. Don't say banishment.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. You are banished from Verona. Be patient. The world is wide.

ROMEO. There is no world outside Verona's walls. Only purgatory, torture, hell itself. Being banished from Verona is being banished from the world, and being banished from the world is death. So "banishment" is just a nicer word for death. By calling death "banishment," you cut off my head with a golden ax and smile at the blow that kills me.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Oh, what deadly sin! What rude ingratitude! The law demanded your death, but the kind Prince, taking your side, pushed the law aside and changed that black word "death" to banishment. This is a great mercy, and you can't see it.

ROMEO. It's torture, not mercy. Heaven is here, where Juliet lives. Every cat, every dog, every little mouse, every unworthy creature lives here in heaven and can look at her. But Romeo cannot. Flies have more honor, more status, more right to court Juliet than Romeo does. They can land on the white wonder of her hand and steal immortal blessings from her lips, which blush in pure modesty as if their own kisses were sinful. But Romeo cannot — he is banished. Flies are free, but I am banished. And you still say exile is not death? Don't you have some poison mixed up, some sharp knife, some quick way to end my life, however lowly, other than "banished"? "Banished"! Oh Friar, the damned in hell use that word, and howling follows it. How can you have the heart, being a man of God, a holy confessor, a forgiver of sins, and my professed friend, to tear me apart with that word "banished"?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. You foolish madman, listen to me for just a moment.
ROMEO. Oh, you're going to talk about banishment again.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. I'll give you armor to protect you from that word — the sweet comfort of philosophy, to console you even though you're banished.
ROMEO. Still "banished"? To hell with philosophy! Unless philosophy can create a Juliet, uproot a town, or reverse a Prince's decree, it's useless. It doesn't help. Don't talk anymore.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Oh, I see that madmen have no ears.
ROMEO. How could they, when wise men have no eyes?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Let me reason with you about your situation.

ROMEO. You can't speak about what you don't feel. If you were as young as I am, with Juliet as your love, married for just one hour, a murderer, lovesick like me, and banished like me — then you could speak. Then you could tear your hair and throw yourself on the ground like I'm doing now, measuring out the grave I'll never fill.
[Knocking within.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Get up! Someone's knocking. Romeo, hide yourself!
ROMEO. No. Not unless the mist of my heartbroken sighs hides me from searching eyes.
[Knocking.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Listen to that knocking! Who's there? Romeo, get up. You'll be caught! Wait a moment. Stand up!
[Knocking.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Run to my study! I'm coming, I'm coming! God's will, what foolishness is this! I'm coming!
[Knocking.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Who's knocking so hard? Where are you from? What do you want?
[Within.] Let me come in, and you shall know my errand.]
NURSE. I come from Lady Juliet.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Welcome, then.
[Enter Nurse.]
NURSE. Oh holy Friar, tell me, holy Friar — where is my lady's husband? Where's Romeo?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. There on the floor, drunk on his own tears.

NURSE. Oh, he's in the same state as my mistress! Exactly the same! Oh, what pitiful sympathy! What a miserable situation! She's lying there too, sobbing and weeping, weeping and sobbing. Stand up, stand up! Stand like a man! For Juliet's sake, for her sake, get up! Why would you fall into such a deep despair?
ROMEO. Nurse!
NURSE. Oh sir, oh sir — death is the end of everything.

ROMEO. Did you just mention Juliet? How is she? Does she think I'm nothing but a murderer now that I've stained the beginning of our happiness with blood so close to her own? Where is she? How is she doing? And what does my secret wife say about our ruined love?
NURSE. Oh, she says nothing, sir. She just weeps and weeps. First she falls on her bed, then she jumps up and cries out for Tybalt, then cries for Romeo, then falls down again.

ROMEO. As if my name, shot from a deadly gun, murdered her, just as the hand belonging to that name murdered her cousin. Oh, tell me, Friar, in what vile part of my body does my name live? Tell me, so I can destroy the hateful place.
[Drawing his sword.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Stop that desperate hand! Are you a man? You look like one, but your tears are womanish, and your wild behavior is more like a mindless beast. You — who seem like a woman in a man's body, and an animal pretending to be both! You've shocked me. By my holy order, I thought you had a better temperament. Have you killed Tybalt? Will you now kill yourself? And kill your wife too, who lives only because you live, by committing this damned act against yourself? Why do you curse your birth, heaven, and earth? Your birth, heaven, and earth all come together in you at once, and you would throw them all away at once. Shame on you! You disgrace your body, your love, and your mind. Like a miser, you're rich in all three but use none of them properly. Your noble body is just a wax figure, falling short of true manhood. Your dear love is nothing but a hollow lie, killing the very love you swore to cherish. Your mind, which should guide both your body and your love, is misshapen in its management of both — like gunpowder in a clumsy soldier's flask, set on fire by your own ignorance, blowing yourself apart with your own defenses. Pull yourself together, man! Your Juliet is alive — the very one whose death would have killed you. So you're lucky there. Tybalt wanted to kill you, but you killed Tybalt. Lucky again. The law that threatened death has been turned to exile. Lucky yet again. A whole pack of blessings has landed on your shoulders. Happiness is courting you in her finest clothes. But like a sulky, stubborn brat, you slap away both Fortune and love. Be careful — people like that die miserable. Go to your love, as planned. Climb to her room and comfort her. But make sure you leave before the night watch is set, because after that you won't be able to get through to Mantua. You'll live there until we can find the right time to announce your marriage publicly, reconcile your families, beg the Prince's pardon, and call you back with twenty hundred thousand times more joy than you had when you left in grief. Go ahead, Nurse. Give my regards to your lady and tell her to get everyone in the house to bed, which their heavy sorrow will make them ready for. Romeo is coming.
NURSE. Oh Lord, I could have stayed here all night listening to such wise counsel! What a thing it is, learning! My lord, I'll tell my lady you're coming.
ROMEO. Do that, and tell my sweet to prepare herself.
NURSE. Here, sir, a ring she asked me to give you. Hurry, go quickly, because it's getting very late.
[Exit.]
ROMEO. How well this revives my spirits!

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Go now. Good night. And here is your whole situation in a nutshell: either leave before the night watch is posted, or at the break of day, get out of here in disguise. Stay in Mantua. I'll find your servant, and he'll bring you news from time to time of every good thing that happens here. Give me your hand. It's late. Farewell. Good night.
ROMEO. Except that a joy beyond all joy calls out to me, parting from you would be a grief so deep. Farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 4 — A Room in Capulet's House
paragraphs: [Enter Capulet, Lady Capulet and Paris.]

CAPULET. Things have turned out so badly that we haven't had time to talk to our daughter about your proposal. You see, she loved her cousin Tybalt very much. And so did I. Well, we were all born to die. It's very late. She won't come downstairs tonight. I promise you, if it weren't for your company, I'd have been in bed an hour ago.
PARIS. These times of grief are no time for courtship. Good night, madam. Give my regards to your daughter.
LADY CAPULET. I will, and I'll find out how she feels first thing tomorrow. Tonight she's locked away with her sorrow.

CAPULET. Sir Paris, I'll make a bold offer of my daughter's love. I believe she'll obey me in everything. In fact, I'm sure of it. Wife, go to her before you go to bed. Tell her about Paris's love, and tell her — listen carefully — that next Wednesday... wait, what day is this?
PARIS. Monday, my lord.

CAPULET. Monday! Ha! Well, Wednesday is too soon. Let it be Thursday. On Thursday, tell her, she'll be married to this noble gentleman. Will you be ready? Is this too rushed? We won't make a big event of it — just a friend or two. Since Tybalt was killed so recently, it would look bad if we celebrated too much, being his relatives. So we'll have just a small gathering. And that's that. What do you think about Thursday?
PARIS. My lord, I wish Thursday were tomorrow.

CAPULET. Well then, it's settled. Thursday it is. Go to Juliet before you go to bed, wife. Prepare her for this wedding day. Farewell, my lord. Lights to my chamber! Good heavens, it's so very late that we might as well call it early. Good night.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 5 — Juliet's Chamber
paragraphs: [Enter Romeo and Juliet.]
JULIET. Are you leaving already? It's not even close to dawn. It was the nightingale you heard, not the lark, singing in that pomegranate tree. Believe me, love, it was the nightingale.

ROMEO. It was the lark, the herald of morning, not the nightingale. Look, love — see those streaks of light lacing the clouds in the eastern sky? The stars of night have burned out, and cheerful day stands on tiptoe on the misty mountaintops. I must go and live, or stay and die.
JULIET. That light is not daylight — I know it. It's some meteor that the sun has sent out to be your torchbearer tonight and light your way to Mantua. So stay. You don't need to go yet.

ROMEO. Let me be caught. Let me be put to death. I'm fine with it, if that's what you want. I'll say that gray light is not the morning sun — it's just the pale reflection of the moon. And that's not the lark whose song beats so high against the sky above us. I'd rather stay than go. Come, death, and welcome! Juliet wants it this way. How are you, my soul? Let's talk. It's not day yet.

JULIET. It is, it is! Hurry! Go! Get away! It's the lark singing so out of tune, making harsh, unpleasant sounds. Some say the lark makes beautiful music, but this one doesn't — it tears us apart. Some say the lark and the ugly toad swapped eyes. Oh, I wish they had swapped voices too, since it's that voice that chases you away from me, hunting you out with the music of the morning. Oh, go now. It's getting brighter and brighter.
ROMEO. More light, more light — and darker and darker our sorrows.
[Enter Nurse.]
NURSE. Madam!
JULIET. Nurse?
NURSE. Your mother is coming to your room. Day is breaking. Be careful! Watch out!
[Exit.]
JULIET. Then, window, let day in and let life out.
ROMEO. Farewell, farewell! One kiss, and I'll climb down.
[Descends.]

JULIET. Are you gone already? My love, my lord, my husband, my friend! I need to hear from you every single day, because every minute feels like many days. Oh, by that count, I'll be ancient before I see my Romeo again.
ROMEO. Farewell! I won't miss any chance to send you my love.
JULIET. Oh, do you think we'll ever meet again?
ROMEO. I don't doubt it. And all these sorrows will become sweet stories we tell each other in the future.
JULIET. Oh God! I have a dark premonition! I seem to see you now, far below me, looking like a dead man in the bottom of a tomb. Either my eyesight is failing, or you look pale.
ROMEO. Trust me, love, you look the same to me. Dry sorrow drains the color from our faces. Goodbye, goodbye!
[Exit below.]

JULIET. Oh Fortune, Fortune! Everyone calls you fickle. If you are fickle, what are you doing with a man who is famous for being faithful? Be fickle, Fortune! Because then, I hope, you won't keep him long and will send him back to me.
[Within.] Ho, daughter, are you up?]
JULIET. Who's calling? Is that my mother? Why is she still up so late, or up so early? Something unusual must have brought her here.
[Enter Lady Capulet.]
LADY CAPULET. Well, how are you, Juliet?
JULIET. Madam, I am not well.

LADY CAPULET. Still crying over your cousin's death? Are you going to wash him from his grave with tears? Even if you could, you couldn't bring him back to life. So stop. Some grief shows great love, but too much grief shows a lack of wisdom.
JULIET. Yet let me weep for such a deeply felt loss.
LADY CAPULET. By weeping, you'll feel the loss, but not bring back the person you weep for.
JULIET. Feeling the loss so deeply, I can't help but weep for my lost friend.
LADY CAPULET. Well, girl, you weep less for his death and more because the villain who killed him is still alive.
JULIET. What villain, madam?
LADY CAPULET. That villain Romeo.
JULIET. "Villain" and Romeo are miles apart. God forgive him — I do, with all my heart. And yet no man grieves my heart like he does.
LADY CAPULET. That's because the traitorous murderer is still alive.
JULIET. Yes, madam, beyond the reach of my hands. I wish no one but me could avenge my cousin's death.

LADY CAPULET. We'll have vengeance for it, don't worry. Stop crying. I'll send someone to Mantua, where that banished fugitive lives, who will give him such an unusual drink that he'll soon be keeping Tybalt company. And then I hope you'll be satisfied.

JULIET. Indeed, I'll never be satisfied with Romeo until I see him — dead — is my poor heart, grieving for a kinsman. Madam, if you could find a man to carry a poison, I would mix it myself, so that Romeo, upon receiving it, would soon sleep peacefully. Oh, how my heart hates to hear his name and not be able to go to him, to pour out the love I had for my cousin upon his body, the one who killed him.
LADY CAPULET. Find the means, and I'll find the man. But now I have joyful news for you, girl.
JULIET. Joy comes at a good time when it's so badly needed. What is it, my lady?
LADY CAPULET. Well, you have a caring father, child. To lift you out of your sadness, he has arranged a sudden day of happiness that you don't expect and I didn't look for.
JULIET. Madam, what day is that?
LADY CAPULET. Well, child, early next Thursday morning, the gallant, young, and noble Count Paris will make you a joyful bride at Saint Peter's Church.

JULIET. By Saint Peter's Church, and by Peter himself, he will not make me a joyful bride! I'm amazed at this rush — that I should marry before the man who's supposed to be my husband has even courted me. Please tell my father, madam, I will not marry yet. And when I do, I swear it will be to Romeo — whom you know I hate — rather than to Paris. Now there's some news for you!
LADY CAPULET. Here comes your father. Tell him yourself and see how he takes it.
[Enter Capulet and Nurse.]

CAPULET. When the sun sets, the air becomes damp with dew. But for the death of my brother's son, it rains outright. What's this? Still in tears? Still pouring? In one small body, you're playing the part of a ship, a sea, and a wind all at once. Your eyes are the sea, ebbing and flowing with tears. Your body is the ship, sailing through this flood of salt water. Your sighs are the winds, raging along with your tears. Without a sudden calm, they'll capsize your storm-tossed body. How about it, wife? Have you told her our decision?
LADY CAPULET. Yes, sir. But she refuses. She says thank you, but no. I wish the fool were married to her grave!

CAPULET. Wait. Explain this to me, wife. What do you mean, she refuses? Isn't she grateful? Isn't she proud? Doesn't she count herself blessed — unworthy as she is — that we've arranged for such a worthy gentleman to be her husband?
JULIET. Not proud of what you've done, but grateful that you did it. I can never be proud of what I hate, but I can be thankful even for hate when it's meant with love.

CAPULET. What is this? What kind of twisted logic? "Proud" and "I thank you" and "I don't thank you" and "not proud"? Listen here, you spoiled little girl. Don't "thank" me and don't "proud" me. Just get your pretty self ready for next Thursday to go with Paris to Saint Peter's Church. Or I will drag you there on a cart! Out, you pale-faced wretch! Out, you worthless girl! You pasty-face!
LADY CAPULET. Stop it! What, have you gone mad?
JULIET. Good father, I beg you on my knees — hear me out. Just let me say one word.

CAPULET. Hang you, disobedient wretch! I'm telling you this: get yourself to church on Thursday, or never look me in the face again. Don't speak, don't reply, don't answer me! My fingers itch to hit you. Wife, we barely thought ourselves blessed that God gave us only this one child. But now I see this one child is one too many, and having her is a curse. Get out of my sight, you worthless girl!
NURSE. God in heaven bless her! You're wrong, my lord, to scold her so harshly.
CAPULET. And why is that, Lady Wisdom? Hold your tongue! Save your clever words for the gossips over a bowl of punch. We don't need them here.
NURSE. I'm not saying anything wrong.
CAPULET. Oh, for God's sake!
NURSE. Can't a person speak?
CAPULET. Quiet, you mumbling fool! Save your wisdom for the gossips at a tea party. We don't need it here.
LADY CAPULET. You're getting too heated.

CAPULET. God's bread, it drives me mad! Day, night, every hour, whether at work or at play, alone or in company, my constant concern has been to find her a good match. And now that I've provided a gentleman of noble birth, fine estates, youth, noble connections, and packed with admirable qualities — as well proportioned as anyone could wish — now this wretched, whining doll, when fortune comes knocking, answers, "I won't marry. I can't love. I'm too young. Please forgive me." Well, if you won't marry, I'll forgive you, all right. Go graze wherever you like, but you will not live under my roof. Think about it. I mean it. Thursday is near. Put your hand on your heart and consider carefully. If you're mine, I'll give you to my friend. If you're not, then hang, beg, starve, and die in the streets! Because I swear on my soul, I'll never acknowledge you again, and nothing I own will ever benefit you. Trust me on that. Think it over. I won't go back on my word.
[Exit.]

JULIET. Is there no pity in heaven that can see to the bottom of my grief? Oh, sweet mother, don't cast me aside! Delay this marriage for a month, a week! Or, if you won't, make my bridal bed in that dark tomb where Tybalt lies.
LADY CAPULET. Don't talk to me. I won't say a word. Do what you want. I'm done with you.
[Exit.]

JULIET. Oh God! Oh Nurse, how can this be prevented? My husband is on earth, and my marriage vow is registered in heaven. How can that vow come back to earth unless my husband sends it from heaven by dying? Comfort me! Advise me! It's terrible that heaven should use such schemes against someone as defenseless as me. What do you say? Don't you have one word of hope? Some comfort, Nurse.

NURSE. Well, here it is. Romeo is banished, and I'd bet everything that he'll never dare come back to claim you. Or if he does, it'll have to be in secret. So, since things stand as they do, I think you'd be best off marrying the Count. Oh, he's a lovely gentleman! Romeo is a dishcloth compared to him. An eagle, madam, doesn't have eyes so bright, so quick, or so beautiful as Paris has. Curse my heart, but I think you'd be happy in this second marriage. It's better than the first. Or if it isn't, your first husband is dead — or as good as dead, since he's banished and no use to you.
JULIET. Do you speak from your heart?
NURSE. And from my soul too. Or curse them both.
JULIET. Amen.
NURSE. What?
JULIET. Well, you've comforted me tremendously. Go inside and tell my mother I've gone — having displeased my father — to Friar Lawrence's cell, to make confession and be forgiven.
NURSE. I will. That's a wise decision.
[Exit.]

JULIET. You damned old woman! You wicked traitor! Is it a greater sin to wish me to break my vow, or to insult my husband with the same tongue that has praised him a thousand times beyond compare? Go away, advisor. From now on, you and my heart are strangers. I'll go to the Friar and ask for his remedy. If all else fails, I have the power to die.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 1 — Friar Lawrence's Cell
paragraphs: [Enter Friar Lawrence and Paris.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. On Thursday, sir? That's very little time.
PARIS. My father-in-law Capulet wants it this way, and I'm not about to slow things down.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. You say you don't know how the lady feels about it. This is an uneven course. I don't like it.

PARIS. She weeps constantly for Tybalt's death, and so I've barely talked to her about love. Venus doesn't smile in a house of mourning. Now her father thinks it's dangerous for her to give in so completely to grief. In his wisdom, he's rushing our marriage to stop the flood of her tears, which, left alone with too much brooding, may only get worse. Now you know the reason for this haste.
[Aside.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. I wish I didn't know why it should be delayed. Look, sir, here comes the lady toward my cell.
[Enter Juliet.]
PARIS. What a happy meeting, my lady and my future wife!
JULIET. That may be true, sir, when I actually become a wife.
PARIS. That will be, and must be, love, next Thursday.
JULIET. What must be, will be.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. That's certainly true.
PARIS. Have you come to make confession to the Friar?
JULIET. To answer that question, I'd have to confess to you.
PARIS. Don't deny to him that you love me.
JULIET. I will confess to you that I love him.
PARIS. And I'm sure you'll also confess that you love me.
JULIET. If I do, that confession will mean more when spoken behind your back than to your face.
PARIS. Poor darling, your face has been terribly abused by tears.
JULIET. The tears haven't won much of a victory. My face was bad enough before they attacked it.
PARIS. You're being too hard on your face — worse than the tears.
JULIET. That's not slander, sir, when it's the truth. And what I said, I said to my own face.
PARIS. Your face is mine, and you've slandered it.
JULIET. That may be, since it doesn't feel like my own anymore. Are you free now, holy Father, or should I come back at evening mass?
FRIAR LAWRENCE. I'm free now, my thoughtful daughter. My lord, we need a moment alone.
PARIS. God forbid I should interrupt her devotions! Juliet, I'll wake you early on Thursday. Until then, farewell, and keep this holy kiss.
[Exit.]
JULIET. Oh, shut the door! And when you've done that, come weep with me. I'm past hope, past cure, past help!
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Oh Juliet, I already know your grief. It pushes me beyond the limits of my wisdom. I hear you must — and nothing can delay it — be married to this Count on Thursday.

JULIET. Don't tell me, Friar, that you've heard about this unless you can also tell me how to prevent it. If your wisdom can't help me, just call my decision wise, and with this knife I'll solve it right now. God joined my heart to Romeo's, and you joined our hands. Before this hand, sealed to Romeo by you, becomes bound to another man, or my true heart turns traitor to another, this knife will kill us both. So out of your long experience, give me some counsel now, or watch this bloody knife settle the matter that all your years and wisdom couldn't resolve. Don't take long to speak. I long to die if what you say offers no remedy.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Wait, daughter. I do see a glimmer of hope, but it requires an execution as desperate as the situation we're trying to prevent. If you have the courage to kill yourself rather than marry Count Paris, then you'll likely have the courage to undergo something that resembles death, to escape from this shame. If you dare, I'll give you the solution.

JULIET. Oh, tell me to jump off the battlements of a tower rather than marry Paris! Tell me to walk through alleyways full of thieves, or to hide where serpents lurk. Chain me up with roaring bears. Shut me in a crypt at night, piled high with dead men's rattling bones, with rotting limbs and yellow skulls. Or tell me to climb into a freshly dug grave and hide under a dead man's burial shroud. Things that, just hearing them described, make me tremble — I'll do them without fear or hesitation to remain a faithful wife to my sweet love.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Then hold on. Go home, act cheerful, and agree to marry Paris. Wednesday is tomorrow. Tomorrow night, make sure you sleep alone. Don't let the Nurse sleep in your room. Take this vial, and once you're in bed, drink the liquid inside. Immediately a cold, drowsy sensation will spread through your veins. Your pulse will stop. No warmth, no breath will show you're alive. The color in your lips and cheeks will fade to pale ash. Your eyes will close like shutters when death seals up the light of life. Every part of your body will stiffen and become cold, appearing to be dead. And in this borrowed appearance of death, you'll remain for forty-two hours, then wake as if from a pleasant sleep. When the bridegroom comes in the morning to wake you from bed, you'll appear to be dead. Then, as is our custom, dressed in your finest clothes, uncovered on a funeral bier, you'll be carried to the ancient vault where all the Capulets are buried. Meanwhile, I'll send letters to Romeo telling him our plan, and he'll come here. He and I will be there when you wake, and that very night Romeo will take you away to Mantua. This will free you from the present disaster, if no fickle fear or womanish weakness weakens your resolve when it's time to act.
JULIET. Give it to me! Give it to me! Don't speak to me of fear!
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Wait. Go now. Be strong and committed to this plan. I'll send a friar quickly to Mantua with my letters to your husband.
JULIET. Love, give me strength, and strength will see me through. Farewell, dear Father.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 2 — Hall in Capulet's House
paragraphs: [Enter Capulet, Lady Capulet, Nurse and Servants.]
CAPULET. Invite as many guests as are on that list.
[Exit first Servant.]
CAPULET. You there, go hire me twenty skilled cooks.
SECOND SERVANT. You won't get any bad ones, sir. I'll test them by seeing if they can lick their own fingers.
CAPULET. How does that test them?
SECOND SERVANT. Well, sir, any cook who won't taste his own food isn't worth hiring. So anyone who can't lick his fingers doesn't come with me.
CAPULET. Fine, go on then.
[Exit second Servant.]
CAPULET. We'll be short on preparations at this rate. Has my daughter gone to see Friar Lawrence?
NURSE. Yes, indeed.
CAPULET. Well, maybe he can do her some good. She's been a stubborn, willful little brat.
[Enter Juliet.]
NURSE. Look, here she comes from confession with a cheerful face.
CAPULET. Well now, my headstrong girl! Where have you been running off to?

JULIET. Where I learned to repent the sin of disobedience toward you and your commands. Holy Friar Lawrence has instructed me to fall on my knees before you and beg your forgiveness. Forgive me, I beg you. From now on, I will always do as you say.
CAPULET. Send for the Count! Go tell him about this! I'll have this marriage arranged for tomorrow morning!
JULIET. I met the young lord at Lawrence's cell and gave him what proper expressions of love I could, without overstepping the bounds of modesty.
CAPULET. Well, I'm glad to hear it! This is how it should be. Let me see the Count. Yes, indeed! Go, I say, and bring him here. Before God, this good holy Friar — our whole city owes him a debt.
JULIET. Nurse, will you come with me to my room to help me pick out the clothes and accessories you think are right for tomorrow?
LADY CAPULET. No, not until Thursday. There's time enough.
CAPULET. Go, Nurse, go with her. We'll go to church tomorrow.
[Exeunt Juliet and Nurse.]
LADY CAPULET. We'll be short on food and supplies. It's nearly nighttime already.

CAPULET. Nonsense! I'll take care of everything, and it will all turn out fine, I promise you, wife. Go to Juliet and help her get dressed. I won't go to bed tonight. Let me handle things. I'll play the housewife just this once. Hello there! They're all out. Well, I'll walk over to Count Paris myself to prepare him for tomorrow. My heart feels wonderfully light, now that this wayward girl has come around.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 3 — Juliet's Chamber
paragraphs: [Enter Juliet and Nurse.]

JULIET. Yes, those clothes are best. But, gentle Nurse, please leave me alone tonight. I need to say many prayers to ask heaven to smile on my situation, which, as you know, is troubled and full of sin.
[Enter Lady Capulet.]
LADY CAPULET. Still busy? Do you need my help?

JULIET. No, madam. We've picked out everything we need for tomorrow. So please, let me be left alone now, and let the Nurse stay up with you tonight. I'm sure you have your hands full with all this sudden preparation.
LADY CAPULET. Good night. Get to bed and rest. You'll need it.
[Exeunt Lady Capulet and Nurse.]

JULIET. Farewell. God knows when we'll meet again. A faint, cold fear runs through my veins and almost freezes the warmth of life. I'll call them back to comfort me. Nurse! — No. What good would she do here? I must act out this grim scene alone. Come, vial. What if this potion doesn't work at all? Will I be married tomorrow morning, then? No! No! This knife will prevent it. Lie there, just in case.
[Laying down her dagger.]

JULIET. What if the Friar has secretly given me a real poison to kill me, so he won't be disgraced for having married me to Romeo first? I'm afraid of that. And yet, it shouldn't be — he's always been known as a holy man. What if, when I'm placed in the tomb, I wake up before Romeo comes to rescue me? That's a terrifying thought! Won't I suffocate in that vault, with no fresh air to breathe, and die strangled before Romeo arrives? Or if I survive, isn't it likely that the horrible thought of death and darkness, combined with the terror of the place — an ancient crypt where hundreds of years' worth of my ancestors' bones are packed, where bloody Tybalt, freshly buried, lies rotting in his shroud, where they say ghosts walk at certain hours of the night — oh God, isn't it likely that, waking so early among those horrible smells and shrieks like mandrake roots torn from the earth (that drive the living mad who hear them), that I'll go insane, surrounded by all these hideous terrors? Will I madly play with my ancestors' bones and pull mangled Tybalt from his shroud? And in my madness, will I grab some great kinsman's bone and use it as a club to bash in my own desperate brains? Oh look — I think I see my cousin's ghost, searching for Romeo, whose sword pierced his body. Stop, Tybalt, stop! Romeo, Romeo, Romeo! Here's a drink — I drink to you!
[Throws herself on the bed.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 4 — Hall in Capulet's House
paragraphs: [Enter Lady Capulet and Nurse.]
LADY CAPULET. Here, take these keys and get more spices, Nurse.
NURSE. They're asking for dates and quinces in the pastry kitchen.
[Enter Capulet.]
CAPULET. Come on, hurry, hurry! The rooster has crowed twice. The curfew bell has rung. It's three in the morning. See to the baked goods, good Angelica. Spare no expense.
NURSE. Go on, you fussy man, go! Get yourself to bed. You'll be sick tomorrow from staying up all night.
CAPULET. Not a bit! I've stayed up all night before for less important things and never gotten sick.
LADY CAPULET. Yes, you were quite the night owl in your time. But I'll keep you from that kind of late-night activity now.
[Exeunt Lady Capulet and Nurse.]
CAPULET. You jealous thing, you!
[Enter Servants, with spits, logs and baskets.]
CAPULET. Now, fellow, what do you have there?
FIRST SERVANT. Things for the cook, sir. But I don't know what exactly.
CAPULET. Hurry up, hurry up!
[Exit First Servant.]
CAPULET. You there — get drier logs. Call Peter. He'll show you where they are.
SECOND SERVANT. I've got a head on my shoulders, sir, that can find logs without bothering Peter.
[Exit.]

CAPULET. Ha! Well said! A funny fellow. You'll end up the blockhead, though. Good heavens, it's daylight already! The Count will be here any minute with his musicians. He said he would. I can hear him approaching.
[Play music.]
CAPULET. Nurse! Wife! Hello! What, Nurse, I say!
[Re-enter Nurse.]
CAPULET. Go wake Juliet. Go get her dressed and ready. I'll go chat with Paris. Hurry, hurry! The bridegroom is already here. Hurry, I say!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 5 — Juliet's Chamber
paragraphs: [Enter Nurse.]

NURSE. Mistress! What, mistress! Juliet! Fast asleep, I'm sure. Come on, lamb! Come on, lady! You lazy thing! Come on, sweetheart! Come on, bride! Not a word? Taking your rest while you can, I see. Sleep for the whole week if you want, because tomorrow night, Count Paris will make sure you don't get much rest. God forgive me! Indeed and amen! How sound asleep she is! I have to wake her. Madam! Madam! Madam! Go on, let the Count find you in bed — he'll wake you up, all right! Won't you get up? What, dressed in your clothes and lying back down again? I have to wake you up. My lady! My lady! My lady! Oh no! Oh no! Help, help! My lady is dead! Oh, curse the day I was ever born! Somebody bring brandy! My lord! My lady!
[Enter Lady Capulet.]
LADY CAPULET. What's all this noise?
NURSE. Oh, what a terrible day!
LADY CAPULET. What's the matter?
NURSE. Look, look! Oh, what a dreadful day!
LADY CAPULET. Oh no! Oh no! My child, my only life! Wake up, look up, or I'll die with you! Help! Help! Call for help!
[Enter Capulet.]
CAPULET. For shame, bring Juliet out! Her husband is here!
NURSE. She's dead! She's gone! She's dead! Oh, what a day!
LADY CAPULET. What a day! She's dead! She's dead! She's dead!

CAPULET. What! Let me see her! Oh no! She's cold. Her blood has settled and her joints are stiff. Life and these lips parted long ago. Death lies on her like an early frost on the sweetest flower of the field.
NURSE. Oh, what a terrible day!
LADY CAPULET. Oh, what a sorrowful time!
CAPULET. Death has taken her from me to make me weep. It ties up my tongue and won't let me speak.
[Enter Friar Lawrence and Paris with Musicians.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Come, is the bride ready to go to church?

CAPULET. Ready to go, but never to return. Oh, son, the night before your wedding day, Death has taken your bride. There she lies — a flower, taken by Death. Death is my son-in-law, death is my heir. Death has married my daughter. I will die and leave him everything. Life, living — it all belongs to death now.
PARIS. I waited so long to see this morning, and does it give me a sight like this?

LADY CAPULET. Cursed, unhappy, wretched, hateful day! The most miserable hour that time has ever witnessed in its long journey. Only one, just one poor loving child — one thing to find joy and comfort in — and cruel death has snatched it from my sight!

NURSE. Oh sorrow! Oh sorrowful, sorrowful day! The most terrible day, the most sorrowful day I have ever seen! Oh day! Oh day! Oh hateful day! There has never been a day as black as this. Oh sorrowful day! Oh sorrowful day!
PARIS. Cheated, divorced, wronged, scorned, killed! Most hateful death, you've cheated me! Cruel, cruel death has struck me down completely! Oh love! Oh life! Not life, but love in death!

CAPULET. Scorned, grieved, hated, martyred, killed! Merciless time, why did you come now, to murder our celebration? Oh child! Oh child! My soul, not merely my child! You are dead! My child is dead, and with my child, all my joy is buried!

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Peace, for shame! Grief's cure does not lie in this kind of outpouring. Heaven and you both had a share in this fair girl. Now heaven has all of her, and that is better for her. You could not keep your part of her from death, but heaven keeps its part in eternal life. The most you wanted was to see her rise in the world. That was your heaven — that she should advance. Now weep because she has advanced above the clouds, as high as heaven itself? Oh, in your love, you love your child so poorly that you go mad when you see she is well. The woman who lives married for a long time is not best married. The one who dies married young is best married. Dry your tears and place your rosemary on this beautiful body. As is our custom, dress her in her finest and carry her to church. Though our foolish nature tells us to weep, reason sees through nature's tears and finds cause for acceptance.

CAPULET. Everything we prepared for the celebration must now be turned to funeral rites. Our instruments become mourning bells. Our wedding feast becomes a burial dinner. Our joyful hymns change to gloomy dirges. Our bridal flowers serve for a buried body. Everything is reversed.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Sir, go inside. And madam, go with him. And you, Sir Paris. Everyone prepare to follow this beautiful body to its grave. The heavens are frowning on you for some wrong. Don't anger them further by fighting against their will.
[Exeunt Capulet, Lady Capulet, Paris and Friar.]
FIRST MUSICIAN. Well, we might as well pack up our instruments and go.
NURSE. Good fellows, please, pack up. You know this is a pitiful situation.
FIRST MUSICIAN. That it is, truly. Though the situation could be improved.
[Exit Nurse.]
[Enter Peter.]
PETER. Musicians! Oh, musicians! Play "Heart's Ease"! "Heart's Ease"! Oh, if you want me to live, play "Heart's Ease"!
FIRST MUSICIAN. Why "Heart's Ease"?
PETER. Oh, musicians, because my heart itself is playing "My Heart Is Full of Sorrow." Oh, play me some cheerful tune to comfort me.
FIRST MUSICIAN. No cheerful tunes from us. This is no time for music.
PETER. You won't, then?
FIRST MUSICIAN. No.
PETER. Then I'll give it to you good.
FIRST MUSICIAN. What will you give us?
PETER. No money, that's for sure, but mockery! I'll call you minstrels!
FIRST MUSICIAN. Then I'll call you a serving boy.
PETER. Then I'll put my serving knife against your head. I won't take any nonsense from you. I'll "re" you and I'll "fa" you. Do you hear me?
FIRST MUSICIAN. If you "re" us and "fa" us, you're making a note of us.
SECOND MUSICIAN. Please put away your knife and bring out your wit instead.

PETER. All right then, have at you with my wit! I'll beat you senseless with an iron wit and put away my iron knife. Answer me like men: "When gripping grief wounds the heart, and gloomy despair weighs down the mind, then music with her silver sound" — why "silver sound"? Why "music with her silver sound"? What do you say, Simon Catling?
FIRST MUSICIAN. Well, sir, because silver has a sweet sound.
PETER. Nonsense! What do you say, Hugh Rebeck?
SECOND MUSICIAN. I say "silver sound" because musicians play for silver coins.
PETER. Nonsense to you, too! What do you say, James Soundpost?
THIRD MUSICIAN. Honestly, I don't know what to say.

PETER. Oh, excuse me — you're the singer, not the talker. I'll answer for you. It's "music with her silver sound" because musicians have no gold to make a sound with. "Then music with her silver sound brings speedy help and sweet redress."
[Exit.]
FIRST MUSICIAN. What an annoying fool that one is!
SECOND MUSICIAN. Forget him. Come on, let's go inside, wait for the mourners, and stay for dinner.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act V, Scene 1 — Mantua, a Street
paragraphs: [Enter Romeo.]

ROMEO. If I can trust the hopeful visions of sleep, my dreams predict some joyful news is coming. My heart feels light, and all day long an unusual energy has lifted me up with cheerful thoughts. I dreamed my lady came and found me dead — a strange dream, to let a dead man think! — and breathed such life into me with her kisses that I came back to life and became an emperor. Ah, how sweet love itself must be, when even the shadows of love are so rich with joy!
[Enter Balthasar.]

ROMEO. News from Verona! How are you, Balthasar? Have you brought me letters from the Friar? How is my lady? Is my father well? How is my Juliet? I ask again because nothing can be wrong if she is well.

BALTHASAR. Then she is well, and nothing can be wrong. Her body sleeps in the Capulet tomb, and her immortal soul lives with the angels. I saw her laid in her family's vault and immediately rode here to tell you. Forgive me for bringing this terrible news, since you left it as my duty, sir.
ROMEO. Is it really so? Then I defy you, stars! You know where I'm staying. Get me ink and paper, and hire fast horses. I'm leaving tonight.
BALTHASAR. I beg you, sir, be patient. You look pale and wild, as if something terrible is about to happen.
ROMEO. Nonsense, you're wrong. Leave me and do what I told you to do. Do you have any letters from the Friar?
BALTHASAR. No, my lord.
ROMEO. It doesn't matter. Get going and hire those horses. I'll be with you shortly.
[Exit Balthasar.]

ROMEO. Well, Juliet, I will lie with you tonight. Let me think of how. Oh, trouble, you're quick to enter the thoughts of desperate men! I remember an apothecary who lives around here, whom I noticed recently, in ragged clothes, with heavy brows, picking through medicinal herbs. He looked starved, worn down to the bone by poverty. In his shabby shop, a tortoise shell hung on the wall, a stuffed alligator, and skins of strange fish. On his shelves, a pitiful collection of empty boxes, green clay pots, animal bladders, and musty seeds. Scraps of string and old dried rose petals were thinly scattered around to make the place look stocked. Noticing his poverty, I said to myself, if a man ever needed poison — the sale of which is punishable by death in Mantua — here's a miserable wretch who'd sell it to him. That thought was a premonition of what I'd need, and this desperate man must sell it to me. As I remember, this should be his shop. Being a holiday, the poor man's shop is closed. Hello! Apothecary!
[Enter Apothecary.]
APOTHECARY. Who's calling so loud?

ROMEO. Come here, man. I can see you're poor. Here, take forty gold coins. Give me a dose of poison, something fast-acting that will spread through every vein, so that the weary person who takes it falls dead instantly, and the body stops breathing as violently as gunpowder fires from a cannon.
APOTHECARY. I have such deadly drugs, but Mantua's law punishes with death anyone who sells them.

ROMEO. Are you so poor and wretched and afraid to die? Starvation is in your cheeks. Need and desperation stare from your eyes. Contempt and beggary hang on your back. The world isn't your friend, and neither is the world's law. The world offers no law to make you rich. So don't be poor — break the law and take this money.
APOTHECARY. My poverty agrees, even though my conscience does not.
ROMEO. I'm paying your poverty, not your conscience.
APOTHECARY. Put this in any liquid and drink it. Even if you had the strength of twenty men, it would kill you instantly.

ROMEO. There's your gold — a worse poison to men's souls, committing more murder in this ugly world than these poor compounds you're not allowed to sell. I'm selling you poison; you haven't sold me any. Farewell. Buy food and put some flesh on your bones. Come, medicine, not poison — come with me to Juliet's grave, because that's where I must use you.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act V, Scene 2 — Friar Lawrence's Cell
paragraphs: [Enter Friar John.]
FRIAR JOHN. Holy Franciscan Friar! Brother!
[Enter Friar Lawrence.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. That sounds like Friar John's voice. Welcome back from Mantua! What does Romeo say? Or if he wrote his thoughts down, give me his letter.

FRIAR JOHN. I went to find a fellow friar to go with me. I found him here in the city, visiting the sick. But the city health officials, suspecting that we'd both been in a house infected with the plague, sealed the doors and wouldn't let us leave. So I was prevented from traveling to Mantua.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Then who delivered my letter to Romeo?
FRIAR JOHN. I couldn't send it — here it is, returned — and I couldn't get a messenger to bring it to you either, because they were all so afraid of the infection.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. What terrible luck! By my brotherhood, that letter was not trivial — it contained information of critical importance, and failing to deliver it could cause great harm. Friar John, go now. Get me an iron crowbar and bring it straight to my cell.
FRIAR JOHN. Brother, I'll go and bring it to you.
[Exit.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Now I must go to the tomb alone. Within three hours, Juliet will wake up. She'll be furious with me that Romeo hasn't heard about the plan. But I'll write to Mantua again and keep her in my cell until Romeo comes. Poor living girl, locked in a dead man's tomb!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act V, Scene 3 — A Churchyard; the Capulets' Monument
paragraphs: [Enter Paris, and his Page bearing flowers and a torch.]

PARIS. Give me your torch, boy. Go stand at a distance. No, put the torch out — I don't want to be seen. Lie down under that yew tree and press your ear to the ground. The soil is loose from all the grave-digging, so you'll hear if anyone approaches. Whistle to warn me if you hear someone coming. Give me the flowers. Now do as I said. Go.
[Aside.]
PAGE. I'm almost too scared to stand here alone in the churchyard. But I'll be brave.
[Retires.]

PARIS. Sweet flower, I scatter flowers on your bridal bed. Oh sorrow — your canopy is dust and stone, which I will water nightly with sweet perfume, or failing that, with tears drawn from my grief. The tribute I will pay you nightly shall be to scatter flowers on your grave and weep.
[The Page whistles.]

PARIS. The boy is warning me — someone is approaching. What cursed foot comes this way tonight, to interrupt my tribute and my rite of true love? Who's that with a torch? Darkness, hide me for a moment.
[Retires.]
[Enter Romeo and Balthasar with a torch, mattock, &c.]

ROMEO. Give me the pickaxe and the crowbar. Here, take this letter. Early tomorrow morning, make sure you deliver it to my father. Give me the light. On your life, I order you: whatever you hear or see, stay at a distance and don't interrupt me. The reason I'm going down into this bed of death is partly to look upon my lady's face, but mainly to take from her dead finger a precious ring, a ring I must use for an important purpose. So go now, leave. But if you're suspicious and come back to spy on what I'm doing next, I swear by heaven I will tear you limb from limb and scatter this hungry churchyard with your body parts. The time and my intentions are savage and wild, more fierce and unforgiving than starving tigers or the raging sea.
BALTHASAR. I'll go, sir, and not trouble you.
ROMEO. That's how you show me friendship. Take this money. Live well and prosper. Farewell, good fellow.
BALTHASAR. All the same, I'll hide nearby. His look frightens me, and I doubt his intentions.
[Retires]
ROMEO. You disgusting stomach, you womb of death, gorged on the most precious morsel the earth has ever known — I'll force your rotten jaws open!
[Breaking open the door of the monument.]
ROMEO. And out of spite, I'll stuff you with more food!

PARIS. This is that banished, arrogant Montague who murdered my love's cousin — and it's believed her grief over that death is what killed her. Now he's come to do some vile desecration to the dead bodies. I'll arrest him!
[Advances.]
PARIS. Stop your unholy work, vile Montague! Can vengeance be pursued beyond death? Condemned villain, I'm placing you under arrest. Obey and come with me, because you must die.

ROMEO. I must die indeed, and that's why I came here. Good, gentle young man, don't tempt a desperate man. Leave this place and go. Think about the dead who lie here and let them frighten you away. Please, young man, don't force me to add another sin to my list by making me furious. Oh, just go! I swear to heaven, I love you better than I love myself, because I came here armed against myself. Don't stay. Go, live. And someday tell people that a madman's mercy told you to run away.
PARIS. I reject your pleas and arrest you here as a criminal!
ROMEO. Are you really going to provoke me? Then have at you, boy!
[They fight.]
PAGE. Oh Lord, they're fighting! I'll go call the watch!
[Exit.]
PARIS. Oh, I'm killed! [Falls.] If you have any mercy, open the tomb and lay me beside Juliet.
[Dies.]

ROMEO. I will, in good faith. Let me look at this face. Mercutio's kinsman, noble Count Paris! What was my servant saying to me as we rode, when my tormented mind wasn't paying attention? I think he told me Paris was supposed to marry Juliet. Did he say that? Or did I dream it? Or am I going mad, hearing talk of Juliet and jumping to that conclusion? Oh, give me your hand, fellow sufferer, whose name is written alongside mine in misfortune's book. I'll bury you in a glorious grave. A grave? Oh no — it's a lantern, slaughtered youth, because Juliet lies here, and her beauty makes this vault a feasting hall full of light. Death, lie here, buried by a dead man.
[Laying Paris in the monument.]

ROMEO. How often, when men are at the point of death, they suddenly become cheerful! Their caretakers call it a burst of energy before death. Oh, how can I call this a burst of energy? Oh my love, my wife! Death, who has sucked the honey of your breath, has had no power yet over your beauty. You are not conquered! Beauty's flag still flies crimson in your lips and in your cheeks. Death's pale banner has not been raised there. Tybalt, do you lie there in your bloody sheet? Oh, what greater favor can I do for you than to kill your enemy with the same hand that cut your youth in half? Forgive me, cousin. Oh, dear Juliet — why are you still so beautiful? Should I believe that death itself is in love with you, and that the gaunt, loathsome monster keeps you here in the dark as his lover? I'm afraid of that, so I will stay with you forever, and never leave this palace of darkness again. Here, here I will remain, with the worms that are your chambermaids. Oh, here I will set up my permanent home and shake off the burden of my unlucky stars from this world-weary body. Eyes, take your last look! Arms, take your last embrace! And lips — you doors of breath — seal with a righteous kiss an eternal contract with all-consuming death! Come, bitter guide! Come, foul-tasting leader! You desperate captain, now drive this seasick, weary ship onto the crashing rocks! Here's to my love! [Drinks.] Oh, the apothecary was honest! His drugs work fast. And so, with a kiss, I die.
[Dies.]
ROMEO. Enter, at the other end of the Churchyard, Friar Lawrence, with a lantern, crow, and spade.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Saint Francis, speed my steps! How often my old feet have stumbled at graves tonight! Who's there? Who keeps company with the dead so late?
BALTHASAR. A friend, sir, and someone who knows you well.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Bless you! Tell me, good friend, what is that torch over there that wastes its light on grubs and eyeless skulls? As far as I can see, it's burning in the Capulet tomb.
BALTHASAR. It is, holy sir. And my master is there — someone you care about.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Who is it?
BALTHASAR. Romeo.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. How long has he been there?
BALTHASAR. A full half hour.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Come with me to the vault.
BALTHASAR. I don't dare, sir. My master doesn't know I'm still here. He threatened me with death if I stayed to watch what he was doing.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Stay, then. I'll go alone. I'm filled with dread. Oh, I fear something terrible has happened.
BALTHASAR. As I slept under this yew tree, I dreamed that my master fought with another man, and that my master killed him.
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Romeo! [Advances.] Oh no, what blood is this that stains the stone entrance of this tomb? What do these ownerless, bloody swords mean, lying here in this place of peace?
[Enters the monument.]
FRIAR LAWRENCE. Romeo! Oh, how pale! Who else? What — Paris too? Soaked in blood? What terrible hour is responsible for this catastrophe? The lady is stirring!
[Juliet wakes and stirs.]
JULIET. Oh, welcome sight, dear Friar! Where is my husband? I remember clearly where I'm supposed to be, and here I am. Where is my Romeo?
[Noise within.]

FRIAR LAWRENCE. I hear a noise! Lady, come away from this nest of death, disease, and unnatural sleep! A power greater than anything we can fight has ruined our plans. Come, come away! Your husband lies dead there in your arms, and Paris too. Come, I'll place you in a convent of nuns. Don't stop to ask questions — the watchmen are coming! Come, go, Juliet! I can't stay any longer!
JULIET. Go, leave. I will not go with you.
[Exit Friar Lawrence.]

JULIET. What's this? A cup, closed in my true love's hand? Poison, I see, was his untimely end. Oh, selfish man! You drank it all and left not one friendly drop to help me follow you? I'll kiss your lips. Maybe some poison still clings to them, to let me die with a healing remedy.
[Kisses him.]
JULIET. Your lips are warm!
[Within.] Lead, boy. Which way?]
JULIET. What? Noise? Then I'll be quick. Oh, lucky dagger!
[Snatching Romeo's dagger.]
JULIET. This is your sheath! [Stabs herself.] Rest there, and let me die.
[Falls on Romeo's body and dies.]
[Enter Watch with the Page of Paris.]
PAGE. This is the place. Right there, where the torch is burning.
FIRST WATCH. The ground is bloody. Search the churchyard. Some of you, arrest whoever you find.
[Exeunt some of the Watch.]

FIRST WATCH. What a pitiful sight! Here lies the Count, slain. And Juliet, bleeding, still warm, and newly dead — she who has been buried here for two days. Go tell the Prince. Run to the Capulets. Wake the Montagues. Send others to search.
[Exeunt others of the Watch.]
FIRST WATCH. We can see the scene where these tragedies lie, but we can't determine the true cause of all this misery without more information.
[Re-enter some of the Watch with Balthasar.]
SECOND WATCH. Here's Romeo's servant. We found him in the churchyard.
FIRST WATCH. Hold him safely until the Prince arrives.
[Re-enter others of the Watch with Friar Lawrence.]
FIRST WATCH. THIRD WATCH. Here's a Friar, trembling, sighing, and weeping. We took this pickaxe and this spade from him as he was coming from this side of the churchyard.
FIRST WATCH. Very suspicious. Hold the Friar too.
[Enter the Prince and Attendants.]
PRINCE. What disaster has happened so early this morning that it drags me from my bed?
[Enter Capulet, Lady Capulet and others.]
CAPULET. What could it be that people are screaming about outside?
LADY CAPULET. The people in the street are crying "Romeo!" Some cry "Juliet!" and some "Paris!" And they're all running toward our family tomb.
PRINCE. What is this alarm that startles our ears?
FIRST WATCH. My lord, here lies the Count Paris, slain. And Romeo is dead. And Juliet, who was dead before, is warm and freshly killed.
PRINCE. Search! Find out how this terrible murder happened!
FIRST WATCH. Here is a Friar, and Romeo's slain servant, carrying tools suitable for opening the tombs of the dead.

CAPULET. Oh, heaven! Oh, wife, look how our daughter bleeds! This dagger has found the wrong target — its sheath is empty on the Montague boy's belt, and it's been plunged into our daughter's chest instead.
LADY CAPULET. Oh God! The sight of death is like a bell that summons my old age to the grave.
[Enter Montague and others.]
PRINCE. Come, Montague. You've risen early to find your son laid even lower.
MONTAGUE. My lord, my wife died tonight. The grief of our son's exile stopped her breath. What further sorrow conspires against my old age?
PRINCE. Look, and you'll see.
MONTAGUE. Oh, you reckless boy! What kind of manners is this, to rush to your grave before your father?

PRINCE. Everyone, hold your grief for a moment until we can sort out these mysteries and learn their origin, their source, their true cause. Then I will lead your mourning, even to death if need be. Meanwhile, be patient, and let misfortune serve patience. Bring forward the suspects.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. I am the one with the most involvement and the least power to act, yet the most suspected — given the time and place — of this terrible crime. Here I stand, both to accuse and to defend myself, both condemned and excused.
PRINCE. Then tell us immediately what you know about this.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. I'll be brief, since the time I have left is not long enough for a lengthy tale. Romeo, lying dead there, was husband to Juliet. And she, lying dead there, was Romeo's faithful wife. I married them. The day of their secret wedding was the day Tybalt died, whose untimely death banished the new bridegroom from this city. It was Romeo's banishment — not Tybalt — that Juliet was grieving for. To lift that grief from her, you arranged a marriage to Count Paris against her will. Then she came to me, and with wild, desperate eyes, begged me to find some way to save her from this second marriage, or she would kill herself right there in my cell. So, guided by my knowledge, I gave her a sleeping potion that produced the appearance of death, just as I intended. Meanwhile, I wrote to Romeo telling him to come here tonight and help me take her from her borrowed grave, since the potion's effect would have worn off by then. But the friar who carried my letter — Friar John — was stopped by accident. Just last night, the letter was returned to me. So, alone, at the planned hour of her waking, I came to take her from her family's vault, intending to hide her in my cell until I could get word to Romeo. But when I arrived, a few minutes before she was to wake, I found noble Paris and true Romeo already dead. She woke up, and I begged her to leave and bear this work of heaven with patience. But then a noise frightened me from the tomb, and she, too desperate, would not come with me. It seems she then took her own life. All of this I know. As for the marriage, her Nurse was in on the secret. And if anything in this has gone wrong through my fault, let my old life be sacrificed to the harshest justice.
PRINCE. We have always known you to be a holy man. Where is Romeo's servant? What can he add to this?

BALTHASAR. I brought my master news of Juliet's death. He immediately rode from Mantua to this very place, to this very tomb. He gave me this letter early on and told me to deliver it to his father. Then he threatened me with death if I didn't leave and let him be.
PRINCE. Give me the letter. I'll read it. Where is the Count's Page, the one who called the watch? Boy, what was your master doing here?

PAGE. He came with flowers to scatter on his lady's grave. He told me to stand back, and I did. Soon someone came with a torch to open the tomb, and before long my master drew his sword on him. Then I ran to call the watch.

PRINCE. This letter confirms the Friar's account — the course of their love, the news of her death. And here Romeo writes that he bought poison from a poor apothecary, and came to this vault to die and lie beside Juliet. Where are the enemies? Capulet! Montague! See what a punishment has been laid upon your hatred — heaven has found a way to kill your joys through love! And I, for looking the other way while you feuded, have lost two kinsmen. Everyone is punished.
CAPULET. Oh, brother Montague, give me your hand. This is my daughter's marriage gift — I can ask for nothing more.
MONTAGUE. But I can give you more. I will raise a statue of her in pure gold. As long as Verona bears that name, no statue will be valued as highly as that of the true and faithful Juliet.
CAPULET. And Romeo's statue will stand just as richly beside his lady's. Poor sacrifices to our hatred.

PRINCE. A dark peace comes with this morning. The sun, in sorrow, will not show its face. Go now, to talk more of these sad events. Some shall be pardoned, and some punished. For never was there a story of more woe than this of Juliet and her Romeo.
[Exeunt.]
